canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
PID Motor Speed Controller

CONTROLS • FEEDBACK • MOTORS • TUNING

Difficulty: ###II Beginner-Intermediate | Cost: $15-18 | Time: 1-2 weekends

Why recruiters want to see this: PID control is the single most asked-about concept in controls

engineering interviews. It's used in robotics, automotive, aerospace, manufacturing, HVAC —

essentially every system that needs to maintain a target value. If you can explain P, I, and D terms,

show a step response plot, and discuss tuning methods, you've demonstrated the core skill of controls

engineering.

Build a system that maintains a DC motor at a precise speed using PID control. A rotary encoder

measures actual RPM, the Arduino computes the PID output, and an H-bridge adjusts motor power.

Display setpoint vs actual RPM on an OLED. Use the Arduino Serial Plotter to visualize your control

loop performance — this plot IS your portfolio data.

What you need:

• Arduino Uno — $4

• L298N H-Bridge motor driver — $2

• DC motor with rotary encoder — $5

• 0.96" OLED display (SSD1306) — $3

@1nska  •  6 EE Projects Recruiters Want  •  Page 4

• 10K potentiometer (setpoint dial) — $0.50

• 12V power supply or battery pack — $3

• Breadboard + jumper wires

Skills this proves:

• PID control theory — proportional, integral, derivative terms and what each does

• Feedback systems — measuring output and correcting in real time

• H-bridge motor driving — PWM speed control, direction switching, braking

• Rotary encoders — counting pulses, calculating RPM, interrupt-driven measurement

• System tuning — Ziegler-Nichols method, understanding overshoot and settling time

• Data visualization — plotting setpoint vs actual for tuning analysis

Step-by-step build:

Step 1: Wire the motor and encoder. Connect the motor to L298N output terminals. Connect

encoder output to Arduino D2 (interrupt-capable pin). Use attachInterrupt() to count pulses.

Calculate RPM: (pulses / pulsesPerRev) × (60000 / timeInterval). Print RPM to Serial Monitor to

verify.

// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Nothing stops a scroll like a small four-legged robot walking across a table. Each leg is a little robot arm with its own inverse

kinematics, and walking is the art of moving them in a coordinated rhythm — a gait — while keeping the body balanced over

the feet still on the ground. Build a 12-servo quadruped, solve leg IK, and implement a creep or trot gait, and you have a
machine that walks, turns, and stands up on its own. It is the most ambitious build in this guide, a genuine mechatronics

and control challenge, and the same fundamentals behind every legged robot from research labs to robot dogs.

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
Capture and detect: A camera grabs frames; OpenCV finds the target — simplest via colour segmentation (threshold in

HSV for a coloured ball), or a face or feature detector. The output is a bounding box or centroid in pixel coordinates.

▸

From pixels to error: The target’s horizontal offset from image centre is your steering error; its apparent size is your

range error. Perception has become two numbers a controller can use.

▸

Visual servoing: Feed those errors into control loops: turn toward the target to zero the horizontal error, drive forward or

back to hold the size at a setpoint. The robot now tracks and follows — a control loop closed through a camera.

▸

Latency and robustness: Vision is slow and noisy compared to a sensor: frames take time, detection jitters, lighting

changes ruin colour thresholds. Filtering the detection and tuning gains for the latency are what make tracking smooth.

▸

Stepping up: Swap colour segmentation for a lightweight neural detector (a MobileNet-class model on a Pi) and the
same pipeline tracks people or objects by class — the path to real-world perception.
▸

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Every modern car has tire-pressure sensors that periodically transmit on 315 MHz (North America) or
433 MHz (Europe) — and each transmission includes a unique sensor ID along with pressure and
temperature. They are unencrypted and broadcast whenever the wheels turn, which means a cheap
radio can log them. Researchers have shown TPMS IDs can be used to identify and track vehicles, and
this project lets you see that privacy gap with your own eyes: park near a road, decode the packets,
and watch unique IDs roll past. It is a striking lesson in how much our everyday devices leak — and
exactly the kind of wireless-security insight that automotive and IoT-security teams hire for.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand sub-GHz ISM transmission, OOK/FSK
demodulation, reverse-engineering an undocumented packet format, and the privacy implications of
unencrypted wireless — the core skill set of automotive RF and wireless-security engineering.

→ The job this maps to: automotive RF, wireless security / penetration testing, and
embedded-systems roles — automakers, Tier-1 suppliers, and IoT-security firms.

Legal & ethics: This is a receive-only demonstration of how much your own car leaks — best done
logging your own vehicles. Building a system to track other people by their TPMS IDs is a privacy
violation (and in many places regulated). Observe to understand the problem; do not operate it as a
surveillance tool.

@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Eavesdrop on the Sky   •   Page 7
canonicalDescription.summary:
Reveal that every car driving past silently broadcasts a unique ID — it is not your
phone tracking you, it is your tires | • TPMS transmissions: Each sensor wakes periodically (or on rotation) and transmits a short burst
with its unique 28-32 bit ID, the tire pressure, temperature, and a checksum. The bursts are
unencrypted and repeat every few seconds to a minute.

• 31
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• TPMS transmissions: Each sensor wakes periodically (or on rotation) and transmits a short burst
with its unique 28-32 bit ID, the tire pressure, temperature, and a checksum. The bursts are
unencrypted and repeat every few seconds to a minute.

• 315 vs 433 MHz: North American cars typically use 315 MHz; European and many other markets use
433.92 MHz ISM. You tune the SDR to the right band for your region — the RTL-SDR covers both
easily.

• OOK and FSK modulation: TPMS sensors use on-off keying or frequency-shift keying with
Manchester or differential encoding. The decoder demodulates the chosen scheme, recovers the
bitstream, then aligns to the packet's preamble and sync word.

• Reverse-engineering the format: Different manufacturers pack the fields differently. Tools like
rtl_433 already know dozens of TPMS protocols; decoding a new one means finding the preamble,
the ID field, and how pressure and temperature are scaled — real protocol reverse-engineering.

• Seeing the privacy gap: Because the ID is static and unencrypted, the same car produces the same
ID every time it passes. Logging these is exactly how researchers demonstrated vehicle tracking —
and seeing your own car's IDs appear makes the abstract risk concrete.

Defense hardware has to work after a night at −40, a day in a hot cargo hold, hours of truck vibration, and a drop onto

concrete. MIL-STD-810 is the standard that defines those tests, and you can build a scaled version of the lab: a thermal
chamber that heats and cools, a vibration table driven by a motor or a speaker, and a controlled drop rig, all instrumented,

with the device under test logging whether it survived. Then torture-test something you built and write the report. It is test-

and-evaluation engineering, cross-discipline (thermal, mechanical, electronic), and it turns “I think it’s rugged” into evidence.

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Two steppers that draw anything you give them — coordinated motion and interpolation

A single controlled motor is one thing; making several move together to trace a precise path

lines, curves, and shapes — the same coordinated-motion and interpolation problem at the
heart of 3D printers, CNC machines, and laser cutters. You build the motion controller: parse
a path, break it into synchronised X / Y steps with proper acceleration, and watch the
machine draw. It is a deeply satisfying, visual build that teaches trajectory planning and
multi-axis coordination, a different and essential facet of motor control.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Night vision is the original force multiplier: the side that can see in the dark owns the night.

Real image-intensifier tubes cost thousands, but a digital version is astonishingly cheap — a

camera with its infrared filter removed sees near-IR light your eyes cannot, and an IR illuminator

floods the scene with light that is invisible to everyone but your sensor. Build it into a

monocular with a small display and you can walk through a pitch-black room, read a sign at

30 metres, and watch wildlife that has no idea it is lit. It is a beginner build with a jaw-

dropping demo, and it teaches the sensor and optics fundamentals behind every EO/IR system.
canonicalDescription.summary:
See in total darkness with a camera that watches infrared — and an

illuminator nobody else can see | Silicon sees infrared: A camera’s silicon sensor is sensitive well past visible red into near-

infrared (about 700–1000 nm); manufacturers add an IR-cut filter so daylight colours look

right. Remove it (a “NoIR” camera) and the sensor sees IR.

▸
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
Silicon sees infrared: A camera’s silicon sensor is sensitive well past visible red into near-

infrared (about 700–1000 nm); manufacturers add an IR-cut filter so daylight colours look

right. Remove it (a “NoIR” camera) and the sensor sees IR.

▸

Active illumination: In true darkness there is little IR to see, so you add your own: an array

of 850 nm IR LEDs floods the scene with light invisible to human eyes (a faint red glow at

most) but bright to the sensor. That is active night vision.

▸

Passive vs active: Image intensifiers amplify faint ambient light (passive, no emission);

thermal cameras see heat. Digital IR-illuminated night vision is active — cheap and effective,

but the illuminator can be seen by other IR cameras.

▸

Low-light imaging: Higher sensor gain and longer exposure pull more from the dark at the cost

of noise and motion blur; a fast lens gathers more light. Balancing gain, exposure, and

illuminator power is the core tuning.

▸

The monocular: A small display behind an eyepiece lens shows the live IR video, and everything

mounts in a tube with the camera and illuminator forward — a self-contained device you hold to

your eye.

▸

canonicalDescription.purpose:
The most talked-about piece of modern soldier equipment is the augmented-reality headset: a see-

through display that overlays a compass, waypoints, teammate locations, and sensor alerts onto the

real world, so the wearer never looks down at a map. You can build the core of one. A small bright

display reflected off a half-mirror in front of your eye gives you a see-through HUD; an IMU

compass and a GPS feed it heading and position; a radio brings in teammate positions and alerts.

Turn your head and the bearing to the waypoint slides across your view. It is optics, embedded

systems, and UI design in one build, and the first-person footage is unlike anything else in this

series.

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
The optical combiner: A small bright display is reflected off a half-silvered mirror (a beam

splitter) angled in front of the eye. The mirror passes the real scene and reflects the

display, so the graphics appear overlaid on the world.

▸

Focus and eye relief: A collimating lens between the display and the combiner sets the image’s

virtual distance so it is sharp alongside distant objects. Eye relief and combiner size set

your usable field of view.

▸

Heading and position: An IMU with a magnetometer gives head heading (fused for stability); a

GPS module gives position. From these you compute the bearing and distance to any waypoint or

teammate.

▸

Rendering the HUD: A microcontroller draws a compass tape, a waypoint marker at its relative

bearing, distance, and alert icons — high-contrast, minimal graphics that read at a glance

without cluttering the view.

▸

Bringing in the team: A radio (your mesh node from project 5, or Bluetooth from a phone)

supplies teammate positions and sensor alerts from the sentry or RF station, so the HUD shows

the whole picture.

▸

Why a half-mirror combiner instead of a screen you look at? A HUD only works if the information

sits on the world — you must see through it. A beam splitter reflects the display into your eye

while passing the real scene, so the overlay floats in front of you. A solid screen would block

the view, which defeats the purpose.

→

Why does the display need a collimating lens? Your eye cannot focus on a screen two inches

away. A lens between display and combiner places the image at a comfortable virtual distance,

near infinity, so the overlay and the distant world are in focus together. Without it the HUD

is a blur.

→

Why fuse heading instead of using the magnetometer alone? A magnetometer alone is noisy and

lags, so a compass overlay would jitter and swim as you turn your head. Fusing the gyro (fast,

but drifts) with the magnetometer (slow, but absolute) yields a smooth, stable heading —

essential for a HUD that has to feel locked to the world.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Commercial myoelectric prosthetic hands cost $20,000-$50,000 and offer 2-4 grip patterns. Modern

AI-driven prosthetics like the Ottobock bebionic or Open Bionics Hero Arm offer individual finger

control, but at higher prices and with significant calibration requirements. This project builds a 5-finger

prosthetic hand controlled by 8-channel forearm EMG with per-user CNN classification — the same

architecture used in research-grade prosthetics. Accessibility is the most meaningful application of

biomedical EE, and Medtronic, Abbott, and Össur all have active acquisition appetites in this space.

System Architecture
canonicalDescription.summary:
EMG Prosthetic Hand with Intent Detection

5-finger control from forearm muscle signals. Faster than your own reflex. | • Forearm EMG array: Same 8-channel acquisition as the silent speech project, but with

electrodes placed in a ring around the upper forearm over the flexor digitorum superficialis and

extensor digitorum communis muscles. These muscles control finge
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• Forearm EMG array: Same 8-channel acquisition as the silent speech project, but with

electrodes placed in a ring around the upper forearm over the flexor digitorum superficialis and

extensor digitorum communis muscles. These muscles control finger flexion and extension; their

electrical signals appear at the skin surface as the user attempts to move individual fingers.

• Pre-amp + filter: Same DSP pipeline as silent speech — 20-450Hz bandpass with 60Hz notch.

Critical to remove motion artifact (slow drift below 20Hz) and electromagnetic interference (power

@1nska  •  6 Physical AI Embodiment Projects  •  Page 9

line noise at 60Hz).

• Per-user classifier (CNN): A small convolutional neural network trained on the user's specific

muscle activation patterns. Every person's forearm anatomy differs, so models must be

personalized. The training takes 60 seconds: the system shows the user a finger to flex; user

attempts the motion; system records the EMG pattern. Repeat for all 10 motions (5 fingers ×

flex/extend).

• Intent → finger mapping: Classifier output is a probability distribution over 10 possible motions.

The highest-probability motion is selected; intermediate-probability motions activate proportional

finger angles for smooth, continuous control.

• Servo drivers + 3D-printed hand: 5 servo motors (one per finger) driven by current-controlled

MOSFET drivers. Position feedback from each servo enables PID control. The hand is 3D-printed

using open-source designs (Inmoov, Open Bionics) with TPU tendons providing compliance.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Meta acquired CTRL-labs for nearly $1 billion to build wrist-based gesture input. They have not built

silent speech yet. The reason is simple: their entire platform is locked into wrist EMG, and silent speech

requires reading muscle signals from the neck, jaw, and throat — a completely different body location,

different muscle group, and different ML model. The acquirer for silent speech is Apple, who needs a

private input method for Vision Pro and Siri, or defense contractors who need silent battlefield

communication. This is the flagship project. The one that gets you noticed.

The opportunity: Silent speech has the same demo impact as 'typing without a

keyboard' — but Meta isn't building it. A 3-4 year window exists before they pivot.

This is the project that defines a career or a startup.

System Architecture

canonicalDescription.summary:
Silent Speech Neural Interface

Mouth words silently. AI reads your muscles. Text appears on screen. | • 8 EMG electrodes around the neck and jaw: Specifically placed over the digastric, mylohyoid,

geniohyoid (chin), platysma (neck), and laryngeal muscles. Each muscle activates with different

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• 8 EMG electrodes around the neck and jaw: Specifically placed over the digastric, mylohyoid,

geniohyoid (chin), platysma (neck), and laryngeal muscles. Each muscle activates with different

phoneme groups — labial sounds (P, B, M) light up different muscles than dental sounds (T, D, N)

or velar sounds (K, G).

• ADS1299 simultaneous acquisition: Texas Instruments' gold-standard biosignal ADC. 24-bit

resolution, 8 channels sampled simultaneously at up to 16kSPS. Built-in PGA (programmable gain

amp) with selectable gain from 1x to 24x. Common-mode rejection ratio >100dB. This single chip

replaces what would otherwise be a discrete board with 8 instrumentation amplifiers.

• STM32H7 DSP: The MCU applies bandpass filtering (20-450Hz, the EMG band), notch filtering

(60Hz), and computes spectral features in real-time. Output: a continuous stream of 8-channel

feature vectors at 100Hz.

• Transformer model (EMG → text): A small encoder-decoder transformer (~2-5M parameters)

trained on paired EMG-to-text data. The encoder converts the EMG feature stream into a hidden

representation; the decoder generates the corresponding text. Runs on-device using TensorFlow

Lite Micro or CMSIS-NN.

• Bluetooth output: Decoded text streams to a paired device (phone, computer, AI assistant) via

BLE GATT. Latency from mouthed word to displayed text: under 500ms.

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
I met a Sales Director during a university-organized visit to a robotics company in April 2025. I wasn't

looking for anything. I just added him on WeChat and moved on.

Seven months later, he had moved to KUKA — one of the world’s largest industrial robotics

manufacturers. That "random add" became the reason I had a $30K industrial robot on my campus.

What happened:

I April 2025: University visit to a robotics company. Quick intro. Added on WeChat.

↑ 7 months between first contact and first ask. He changed companies in between. If I hadn't saved the
contact, I'd never have known.

Why this works:

• Most people only network when they need something. By then, it's too late — you're a stranger

asking for a favor

• When you connect early and ask later, you're "that student from the tour" — not a cold pitch

• The contact cost me nothing. It got me access to a robot worth $30,000 from one of the world's

biggest robotics companies

The rule:

Every company visit, networking event, conference, or random introduction — save the contact.

You don't need a reason right now. Your future self will thank you.

I Go to every campus event, company visit, and networking mixer. Exchange contacts with everyone. You
have no idea which one will change your life.

// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

canonicalDescription.purpose:
The 433 MHz ISM band is full of chatter you never notice: wireless weather stations, remote
thermometers, soil-moisture sensors, doorbells, garage remotes, and cheap smart-home gadgets all
transmit there in the clear. Point an SDR at it and an open-source decoder turns that noise into
readable data — temperatures, humidity, button presses, sensor IDs — from devices all around your
neighbourhood and inside your own home. It is the most approachable possible introduction to IoT
reverse-engineering, and the natural gateway to building your own sensor network or auditing what
your devices leak. The same skills underpin IoT product development and wireless security.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand sub-GHz ISM communication, OOK/FSK
demodulation, packet framing and checksums, and decoding undocumented device protocols. This
is exactly the wireless skill set behind IoT product engineering and connected-device security.

→ The job this maps to: IoT / embedded wireless, home-automation, and wireless-security roles —
IoT product companies, smart-home platforms, and security teams.

canonicalDescription.summary:
Decode the invisible chatter of the ISM band — weather stations, doorbells,
thermometers, your own smart-home sensors | • The 433 MHz ISM band: 433.92 MHz is a licence-free band where countless low-power devices
transmit short, simple messages. Because the band is shared and cheap, manufacturers use
unencrypted OOK/FSK with basic framing — easy to receive and decode.
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• The 433 MHz ISM band: 433.92 MHz is a licence-free band where countless low-power devices
transmit short, simple messages. Because the band is shared and cheap, manufacturers use
unencrypted OOK/FSK with basic framing — easy to receive and decode.

• OOK and FSK: Most cheap sensors use on-off keying (the carrier blips on and off) or simple FSK.
The decoder demodulates the carrier into a raw pulse train, then interprets pulse widths as bits
using each protocol's encoding (PWM, Manchester, and so on).

• Packet framing and IDs: A typical message has a preamble, a device ID, the payload (temperature,
humidity, state), and a checksum. The ID lets you tell your neighbour's weather station from your
own; the checksum lets the decoder reject corrupted packets.

• rtl_433 does the heavy lifting: rtl_433 is an open-source decoder that recognises hundreds of
device protocols out of the box. Run it and it auto-identifies known devices, printing manufacturer,
model, ID, and decoded values as JSON you can log or pipe anywhere.

• Decode the unknown: When you hit a device rtl_433 does not know, you capture the raw signal,
study the pulse pattern, and work out the encoding and fields yourself — a clean, self-contained
protocol reverse-engineering project that is genuinely impressive on a resume.

Build a live map of every plane overhead — callsign, altitude, speed — pulled out of
the air onto your screen | • ADS-B on 1090 MHz: Aircraft transponders broadcast 'extended squitter' messages roughly twice a

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• ADS-B on 1090 MHz: Aircraft transponders broadcast 'extended squitter' messages roughly twice a
second containing the 24-bit ICAO address, GPS latitude/longitude, altitude, speed, and callsign.
The signals are unencrypted and standardised worldwide, so any compatible receiver can decode
them.

• Pulse-position modulation: Mode S encodes bits as the position of short pulses within each
microsecond — a 1 Mbit/s pulse-position-modulated stream. The decoder samples fast enough to
distinguish pulse timing, reconstruct the message bits, and check them with a CRC.

• LNA and filter help range: Distant aircraft are weak and the band sits near strong cellular and pager
interference. A 1090 MHz SAW filter plus a low-noise amplifier at the antenna dramatically extends
range — from tens to a couple hundred kilometres line-of-sight.

each message by CRC, and converts the position fields into latitude/longitude. It serves a live

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Before a satellite can point at anything, it has to know which way it is already facing — and the most
accurate way to do that in space is to look at the stars. A star tracker photographs a patch of sky,
identifies the star pattern by matching it against an onboard catalog, and from that computes the
spacecraft's precise 3-axis orientation, accurate to arc-seconds. This is the highest-precision attitude
sensor ever flown, and you can build a working one: a camera with a fast lens, a small computer, and
an open-source lost-in-space plate-solving algorithm that figures out where you are pointed with zero
prior information. Pair it with Project 3's reaction wheel and you have both halves of a real spacecraft's
attitude system — sensing and actuation.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand low-light image sensors and optics (f-number,
exposure), embedded computer vision, star-identification algorithms, and the coordinate-frame math
(quaternions) behind pointing systems. Star trackers are flagship aerospace GNC hardware —
building one signals you can work on real spacecraft guidance.

@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Reach Space   •   Page 13

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• Fast lens + low-light sensor: Stars are dim, so the optics matter most. A fast lens (f/1.4–f/2) gathers
maximum light; a sensitive CMOS sensor (a Raspberry Pi HQ camera or a Sony IMX module) with a
multi-second exposure captures enough stars per frame to identify a pattern. Monochrome and
longer exposure both help.

• Star centroiding: The software thresholds the image to separate stars from background, then
computes the sub-pixel centroid of each star blob. Centroiding to a fraction of a pixel is what gives
the tracker its arc-second accuracy — far finer than the pixel grid itself.

• Pattern matching (lost in space): The key trick: the angular distances between stars form a unique
fingerprint. An open-source solver like Tetra3 hashes these geometric patterns and matches them
against a precomputed catalog — identifying exactly which stars you are looking at with no prior
orientation estimate.

• Attitude solve: Once stars are identified, their known catalog positions (right ascension and
declination) plus their measured pixel positions let the solver compute the rotation that maps one to
the other. The result is the camera's orientation, expressed as a quaternion or rotation matrix.

• Edge compute: All of this runs on a Raspberry Pi (Zero 2 W or Pi 4). The solve takes well under a
second per frame — fast enough to output a continuous attitude estimate, exactly as a real star
tracker feeds a spacecraft's control system.

// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Tell a motor to go to exactly 90 degrees and hold it there — feedback control, built from
scratch

## why this matters

Open-loop, a motor just spins and you have no idea where it actually is. Add an encoder to
measure its position and a PID controller to drive the error to zero, and the motor becomes a
servo: command 90 degrees and it snaps there and holds, resisting if you push it. This is the
single most important skill in motor control and robotics — closing the loop with feedback —
and it is the foundation under every robot joint, CNC axis, and drone. Building your own PID
position controller (rather than buying a servo) is the project that turns “I can spin a
motor” into “I can control motion.”

canonicalDescription.purpose:
AI voice cloning has reached the point where human ears can't tell the difference. But cloned audio has

measurable artifacts: spectral energy gaps in the 2-4kHz range, unnatural phase continuity, and

missing micro-variations that exist in real vocal cords. This project detects those artifacts using pure

analog signal processing — no machine learning model, no microcontroller.

The key insight: Real voices have chaotic, broadband energy with natural spectral

variation. AI clones have suspiciously smooth spectral envelopes because the

synthesis model interpolates between training samples. An analog filter bank can

measure this difference in real time.

System Architecture

AI Voice Cloning Detector

Analog circuit that detects AI-generated voices — no software, no ML model

Cost: ~$15

Difficulty:
Intermediate-Advanced
Build Time: 1-2 weekends | @1nska  •  6 AI-Era EE Projects  •  Page 3

• Microphone + pre-amp: Electret mic with JFET buffer, then an AGC stage (LM386 or OPA344)

to normalize input levels regardless of speaker volume.

• Bandpass filter bank (8 bands): Eight parallel 2nd-orde
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
@1nska  •  6 AI-Era EE Projects  •  Page 3

• Microphone + pre-amp: Electret mic with JFET buffer, then an AGC stage (LM386 or OPA344)

to normalize input levels regardless of speaker volume.

• Bandpass filter bank (8 bands): Eight parallel 2nd-order Sallen-Key bandpass filters covering

200Hz to 8kHz. Each band is ~1 octave wide. Center frequencies: 250, 500, 1K, 1.5K, 2K, 3K,

4.5K, 7KHz.

• Peak detectors: Each filter output feeds a diode peak detector with ~50ms decay time. This

gives a DC voltage proportional to energy in each band.

• Comparator array: Compares adjacent band energies and checks for suspicious gaps. Real

voices: smooth roll-off, adjacent bands within 6dB. AI clones: sharp dips between bands,

especially 2-4kHz.

• Decision logic: If more than 2 adjacent-band ratios exceed threshold, a simple logic gate

(74HC08 AND) triggers the RED LED. Otherwise, GREEN stays lit.

A $20 temperature-controlled iron, 0.8 mm leaded or lead-free solder, flux and a

together for two seconds, feed solder into the joint, not the iron. Twenty j
canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
DO THIS
A $20 temperature-controlled iron, 0.8 mm leaded or lead-free solder, flux and a

practice kit (a $5 through-hole 'skill kit'). Tin the tip, heat the pad and the leg
together for two seconds, feed solder into the joint, not the iron. Twenty joints and

you'll have it.

THE TRAP
Waiting until a project 'needs' soldering. Breadboards fall apart the moment you move
them — soldering is what makes something yours to keep.

YOU'RE DONE WHEN
Your joints look like small shiny cones, not grey blobs, and a soldered LED circuit
works first try.

STEP 05
Measure everything. Multimeter first, oscilloscope later.

your LED circuit and compare with what Ohm's law predicted. Only reach for a scope
when you start caring about signals over time (PWM, serial, audio).

THE TRAP
Guessing. 'It doesn't work' is not a diagnosis. 'Pin 13 is at 4.9 V but the LED anode
is at 0 V' is — and that takes ten seconds with a meter.

YOU'RE DONE WHEN
You debug by measuring before you debug by re-wiring.

STEP 06
Build one real project you actually want to use.

DO THIS
Not a tutorial — something with a job: a plant-moisture alarm, a desk lamp that dims
with a knob, a door sensor that texts you, a temperature logger for your room. Pick
one, make a parts list, build it on a breadboard, then solder it onto perfboard and

put it in a box.

THE TRAP
Ten half-finished projects. One finished thing you use every day teaches more than

ten demos, and it's the one you'll show people.

YOU'RE DONE WHEN
It's been running on your desk for a week and you've fixed at least one thing that

broke.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
A satellite in low orbit crosses the sky in minutes, so to keep a high-gain antenna pointed at it you need
a tracker that moves. This project builds a real azimuth-elevation rotator: two motors aim an antenna, a
microcontroller predicts the satellite's position from its orbital elements, and the antenna physically
slews to follow the pass from horizon to horizon — exactly what a professional ground station does.
Pair it with an SDR and you can hold a lock on a fast-moving satellite and pull down a clean signal a
fixed antenna would lose in seconds. It is the ground half of every space mission, and watching your
antenna hunt across the sky on its own is genuinely striking.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand satellite tracking and orbital prediction
(TLEs/SGP4), azimuth-elevation pointing and motor control, antenna gain and link geometry, and
ground-station automation. The ground segment is a huge part of the space industry, and a working
auto-tracker is a concrete TT&C; and RF skill.

→ The job this maps to: ground segment and TT&C; (telemetry, tracking & command) — satellite
operators, ground-station networks, and RF/antenna teams.

A motorized antenna that locks onto a satellite and physically follows it across the sky | • Predicting where the satellite is: Every tracked satellite has published orbital elements (a TLE —

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• Predicting where the satellite is: Every tracked satellite has published orbital elements (a TLE —
two-line element set). An SGP4 propagator turns those plus the current time into the satellite's
position, which is then converted to an azimuth (compass bearing) and elevation (angle above the
horizon) from your exact location.

• Azimuth-elevation rotator: Two motors — one for azimuth, one for elevation — aim the antenna at
any point in the sky. Geared steppers (or DC motors with position feedback) move the antenna to
the commanded az/el and update continuously as the satellite moves.

• Why a moving antenna at all: A high-gain, directional antenna has a narrow beam, which is what
gives it the gain to hear a weak satellite — but that beam must stay pointed. A fixed antenna trades
gain for coverage; a tracker gives you both by following the target.

• Closing the loop with the SDR: An SDR at the feed receives the downlink while the rotator tracks.
Because the satellite moves fast, you also correct for Doppler shift in software. Accurate pointing
plus Doppler correction keep a solid lock across the whole pass.

• Horizon-to-horizon automation: The controller waits for a predicted pass, slews to the rise point
(AOS), tracks across the sky, and parks at the set point (LOS) — fully automatic. A scheduler can
chain multiple satellites across a day, exactly like an operational ground station.

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• Radiosonde telemetry: A radiosonde (commonly a Vaisala RS41 or Graw type) transmits a
continuous data frame with its GPS latitude, longitude, and altitude plus temperature, humidity, and
pressure, on a frequency in the 400-406 MHz meteorological band. Each launch site uses a known
frequency you can look up.

• Receiving the signal: As the balloon climbs it becomes line-of-sight over a huge area, so reception
is easy at altitude; the hard part is the low-altitude descent and landing. A directional UHF antenna
(a small Yagi) and an LNA help you hold the signal as the sonde drops behind terrain.

• Decoding the frame: Software like radiosonde_auto_rx demodulates the sonde's FSK telemetry,
decodes the frame format for that sonde type, validates it, and outputs live position and sensor data
— often uploading to a tracking map automatically.

• Predicting the landing: Once you have the descent trajectory and the sonde's current position and
altitude, a descent model (accounting for wind drift under the parachute) predicts the landing spot.
The prediction tightens as the sonde nears the ground.

• The recovery: With a predicted landing zone, you drive toward it, switch to a handheld Yagi for the
final direction-finding, and home in on the last-known position. Recovering the payload is the
tangible payoff — and the sonde can be reflashed for your own balloon or tracking experiments.

// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

IMU on the camera measures its attitude hundreds of times a second and two brushless motors, driven smoothly with field-
oriented control, hold it level no matter what the drone does. Build one and your footage goes from home video to broadcast-

smooth. It is mechatronics, control, and the same FOC drive technology behind robot joints — and it is the upgrade that most

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Sensing the camera’s attitude: An IMU mounted on the camera plate reports its pitch and roll at high rate. The
controller’s job is to hold that attitude at the target regardless of what the frame beneath it does.
▸

Gimbal motors and FOC: Gimbal brushless motors are high-pole-count, low-speed motors driven with field-oriented
control for smooth, cogging-free torque at zero speed — exactly what holding a camera still requires.
▸

The stabilisation loop: A PID loop per axis takes the attitude error and commands motor torque to cancel it. Tuning sets

the stiffness and damping: too soft and it wobbles, too stiff and it oscillates.

▸

Balance is everything: If the camera’s centre of mass sits off the motor axes, the motors fight gravity constantly, wasting

torque and ruining smoothness. Mechanical balance on each axis before any tuning is the golden rule.

▸

Isolating vibration: Motor and prop vibration reaches the gimbal through the frame; rubber dampers between drone and

gimbal filter it so the IMU sees camera motion, not airframe buzz.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
A signals station doesn’t hunt one signal; it watches the whole spectrum, all the time. Build a

permanent RF ground station: an SDR on a mast antenna, continuously sweeping the bands, logging

what is on the air, decoding the public signals — aircraft (ADS-B), ships (AIS), weather

satellites, broadcast — and raising an alert when a new emitter appears where there was none. Its

waterfall dashboard becomes your radio picture of the area. It is the receive-only heart of a

signals post, and it feeds the command map with everything that transmits nearby.

range testing, and bridging the data into your HUD and c
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
BUILD NOTE
Don’t write a mesh stack from scratch. Meshtastic-compatible ESP32 LoRa boards with GPS get

you a working encrypted mesh in an afternoon; the engineering is in antennas, placement,

range testing, and bridging the data into your HUD and command map.

NODE 05 · ONLINE

LoRa: A spread-spectrum modulation that trades data rate for range and sensitivity — kilobits

per second over kilometres at milliwatts. Perfect for text and positions, useless for video,

which is the point.

▸

Meshing: Each node relays messages it hears, so a message hops node to node beyond any single

radio’s range. Flooding with hop limits keeps it simple; smarter routing keeps it efficient.

▸

Position sharing: Nodes with GPS broadcast their position periodically; every node keeps a

table of teammates and their last known location — the data that draws dots on a map or a HUD.

▸

Encryption: Messages are encrypted with a shared channel key, so the mesh is private to your

team even though anyone can receive the raw packets.

▸

Range and power: Antenna height and gain, terrain, and transmit power set range; sleep modes

and duty cycling stretch a battery to days. Range testing is where the link budget becomes

real.

▸

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Sound travels farther and faster in water than radio ever could, which is why navies listen. Build a hydrophone from a piezo

element potted in epoxy, drop it in a lake, and you hear propellers, outboards, and the whole underwater soundscape; add a
second hydrophone a known distance away, measure the time difference of arrival, and you get the bearing to the source —

passive sonar, the technique behind anti-submarine warfare and marine monitoring. It is receive-only, cross-disciplinary
(acoustics, transducers, signal processing), and a strikingly different sensing domain from the RF work in the rest of the

series.

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
SP05 · 36.4 °C · ε 0.95

The ram-air canopy: A parafoil is a soft wing — cells inflated by ram air — that glides, so it can be steered. Pull the left
brake line and the left side slows and dips, turning the canopy left; pull both to flare and slow the descent.
▸

Servo steering: Two small servos on the payload box shorten the left and right brake lines. That gives a controller a

heading command — the whole point that makes the drop precise rather than wherever the wind takes it.

▸

Knowing where you are: GPS gives position; a magnetometer and IMU give heading. The controller computes the bearing

to the landing point and the heading error.

▸

Closing the loop: A heading controller steers toward the landing point, correcting for wind drift, and manages the glide so

it arrives high enough to turn into the wind and flare on the final approach — the same logic full-scale systems use.

▸

The drop platform and safety: The payload is lifted by a drone, a kite, or a safe high point, released to deploy the canopy,
then flies itself down. Everything about the test — area, altitude, payload mass — is chosen so a failure lands harmlessly.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Every spacecraft has a brain: the command-and-data-handling (C&DH;) computer that reads the
sensors, runs the housekeeping, packages everything into telemetry, and beams it to the ground while
accepting commands back up. This project builds a working one — a flight-computer stack that
samples its sensors, forms proper telemetry packets, transmits them over a radio link to a ground
station you also build, and decodes them onto a live dashboard. Use the real spacecraft data standard
(CCSDS) for the packets and you have built the same data architecture that flies on actual missions. It
is less flashy than a thruster, but it is the literal nervous system of a satellite — and the flight-software
skill is in high demand.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand command-and-data-handling architecture,
telemetry packetization (CCSDS), reliable serial/radio links, and ground-side decoding and display.
Flight software and C&DH; are central to every space mission, and a working telemetry pipeline is a
standout systems project.

→ The job this maps to: command & data handling (C&DH;) and flight software — satellite primes,
CubeSat companies, and avionics teams.

@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Build a Real Satellite   •   Page 13

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• The C&DH; role: The flight computer is the spacecraft's housekeeper: on a fixed schedule it reads
every sensor (voltages, currents, temperatures, attitude), checks system health, stores data, and
assembles telemetry for downlink — all while listening for commands from the ground. It is the
integration point for every other subsystem.

• Housekeeping telemetry: Your stack samples a set of 'housekeeping' channels — battery voltage,
board temperature, IMU attitude, a packet counter — at a steady rate. This is exactly the data
operators watch to know a real satellite is alive and healthy.

• CCSDS packetization: Spacecraft do not send raw numbers; they wrap data in standardized
packets. The CCSDS space-packet format adds a header (identifying the data type, a sequence
count, a timestamp) and a checksum. Implementing it means your telemetry is structured,
parseable, and corruption-checkable — the way flight data really works.

• The radio link: A simple radio module (a UHF data module, or LoRa for easy range) carries the
packet stream to the ground. You frame the packets for the link, and the ground side detects frame
boundaries, validates checksums, and rejects corrupted packets — the reliability layer every
downlink needs.

• Ground decoding + dashboard: On the ground, software receives the stream, parses the CCSDS
packets back into named values, and plots them live — voltages trending, temperature rising,
attitude changing. Add a command uplink and you can send instructions back, completing a real
telemetry-and-command loop.

// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Your degree teaches you the floor, not the ceiling. If you only learn what's in the syllabus, you'll have the

exact same skills as every other graduate. That's not a competitive advantage — that's a commodity.

What to do instead:

• Use your classes as a starting point, then go 2–3 levels deeper on your own

• If a class covers data structures, go build a project that uses them in a non-trivial way

• If a class covers circuits, go replicate a real product's hardware

• Treat your professors as mentors, not just lecturers — go to office hours with real questions beyond

the curriculum

The mindset shift:

Classes are a map. The territory is what you explore on your own. The students who land the best

internships treat their coursework as 40% of their education — the other 60% is self-directed.

Free resources to go deeper:

• MIT OpenCourseWare — full MIT courses with problem sets and exams

• Stanford CS courses on YouTube — CS229, CS231n, CS106B

• 3Blue1Brown — visual math intuition that makes everything click

• The Feynman Lectures — physics fundamentals explained by a genius

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Your body produces electrical signals measured in millivolts — and it also acts as an antenna
that picks up the mains hum flooding every room, often a thousand times larger than the
signal you want. The instrumentation amplifier is the circuit that solves this: it amplifies
only the difference between two electrodes while rejecting everything they see in common. Add
a driven-reference electrode and careful filtering and suddenly a heartbeat or a muscle
twitch emerges from the noise. This is the single circuit that makes ECG, EMG, and EEG
possible, and building it yourself — rather than buying a module — is what separates people
who understand biosignals from people who plug in a breakout board.

// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Sense a hidden vehicle by the dent it makes in Earth's magnetic field

As-built gradiometer — two matched HMC5883L magnetometers on the ends of a non-magnetic boom, ESP32 + OLED at centre.

cost — ~$52 as built · a two-sensor gradiometer on a non-magnetic boom

## why this matters

A large steel object — a vehicle, a pipe, a ship — distorts the Earth's magnetic field around it, and a sensitive magnetometer can detect that

distortion from a distance, with no contact and no emission. This is magnetic anomaly detection (MAD), used in defense for submarine hunting and

mine detection, and in the civilian world for archaeology, geophysics, and utility locating. Building one teaches you to pull a tiny anomaly out of a

large, noisy background field — a purely passive sensing skill with the same signal-in-noise flavour as the RF work, but in the magnetic domain.

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Don't learn 10 languages at 10%. Learn one at 100%. Recruiters smell generalists from a mile away. The

person who can say "I know Python deeply — here's a complex project to prove it" will always beat the

person who lists 8 languages on their resume but can't build anything meaningful in any of them.

How to pick your stack:

• If you want to build apps: Learn Swift (iOS) or React Native / Flutter (cross-platform). Pair with a

backend like Node.js or Python/Django

• If you want to do AI/ML: Python is non-negotiable. Learn PyTorch or TensorFlow deeply. Know

NumPy and Pandas cold

• If you want to do systems/infra: C/C++ or Rust. Understand memory, concurrency, and operating

systems at a low level

• If you want to do web: TypeScript + React + a backend framework. Learn it end-to-end so you can

build full products solo

The depth test:

Can you build a complete, non-trivial project in your chosen stack without following a tutorial? If yes, you're

deep enough. If no, keep going.

I Pro tip: Read the source code of libraries you use. Understanding how React or PyTorch works under the
hood separates junior developers from engineers.

#2

Gesture-Controlled Robot Arm

SIGNAL PROCESSING • EMBEDDED SYSTEMS • HARDWARE

Why recruiters love this: It combines signal processing, embedded programming, and mechanical

design in one project. It's visually impressive in demos and shows deep understanding of

sensor-to-actuator pipelines.

Build a robotic arm that you control with your forearm muscles. EMG (electromyography) sensors on

your arm detect muscle contractions, an Arduino processes the signals in real time, and servo motors

move the robotic arm to mirror your gestures.

What you need:

• MyoWare 2.0 EMG sensor (or DIY EMG circuit with instrumentation amp)

• Arduino Mega or ESP32

• 4-6 servo motors (SG90 or MG996R for more torque)

• 3D-printed or laser-cut robot arm frame (files available free online)

• Servo driver board (PCA9685) for controlling multiple servos

• 9V battery pack or bench power supply

Skills it proves:

• Analog signal processing — filtering and amplifying biological signals

• Real-time embedded programming with tight timing constraints

• Servo motor control and PWM fundamentals

• Human-machine interface design

• System integration across multiple subsystems

How to build it:

Step 1: Start with the EMG sensor. Connect the MyoWare to your Arduino and read raw muscle

signals. Plot them on the serial monitor to understand the signal patterns when you flex, extend,

and relax.

Step 2: Filter the signal. Implement a moving average filter or bandpass filter in code to clean up

the noisy EMG data. You need clean, reliable threshold detection.

@1nska  •  6 EE Portfolio Projects  •  Page 6

Step 3: Map signals to movements. Define gesture profiles — e.g., light flex = open hand, hard

flex = close grip, wrist rotation = arm rotate. Create a calibration routine that adapts to different

users.

Step 4: Build or assemble the arm. Use a free 3D-printable design (search Thingiverse for 'robot

arm Arduino'). Attach servos to each joint and wire them through the PCA9685 driver board.

Step 5: Connect everything. Write the main control loop: read EMG → filter → classify gesture →

move corresponding servo. Focus on smooth, responsive movement.

Step 6: Demo and document. Record a video of you controlling the arm with your muscles. This

is your portfolio showpiece. Upload code, wiring diagrams, and the demo video to GitHub.

Bonus: Add a second EMG sensor on the other arm for two-handed control, or

implement a simple ML classifier (using TensorFlow Lite on the ESP32) that

recognizes more complex gestures with higher accuracy.

@1nska  •  6 EE Portfolio Projects  •  Page 7

#3

Custom PCB Synthesizer

PCB DESIGN • ANALOG CIRCUITS • AUDIO

Why recruiters love this: PCB design is the #1 practical skill EE employers test for. Designing a

board that actually makes sound proves you can go from schematic to layout to physical product —

the full hardware development cycle.

Design and fabricate a custom PCB that generates audio waveforms (sine, square, triangle,

sawtooth). Add potentiometers for frequency and volume control, and an audio jack output so you can

plug it into a speaker or headphones. It's a functioning musical instrument you designed from scratch.

What you need:

• KiCad (free PCB design software)

• Op-amps (TL072 or LM358)

• 555 timer IC and/or XR2206 function generator IC

• Potentiometers (10K and 100K)

• 3.5mm audio jack, capacitors, resistors

• PCB fabrication service (JLCPCB or PCBWay — under $5 for 5 boards)

Skills it proves:

• Schematic design and circuit analysis

• PCB layout — trace routing, ground planes, component placement

• Analog circuit design — oscillators, filters, amplifiers

• Manufacturing awareness — DFM, tolerances, BOM management

• Debugging physical hardware with oscilloscope and multimeter

How to build it:

Step 1: Design the oscillator circuit. Start in KiCad with a 555 timer or XR2206-based oscillator.

Simulate in LTSpice to verify your waveform outputs before committing to a PCB.

Step 2: Add control circuits. Design potentiometer-based frequency control (variable resistor in

the timing circuit) and a volume control stage using an op-amp attenuator.

Step 3: Add waveform selection. Use a rotary switch or DIP switches to select between

waveform types. Each position routes a different shaping circuit into the output.

@1nska  •  6 EE Portfolio Projects  •  Page 8

Step 4: Layout the PCB. Route your schematic in KiCad's PCB editor. Keep analog and digital

sections separated, use proper ground planes, and keep trace widths appropriate for audio

signals.

Step 5: Order and assemble. Send gerber files to JLCPCB. While waiting, order components.

When boards arrive, hand-solder components and test each section incrementally.

Step 6: Test and tune. Use an oscilloscope to verify waveform shape, frequency range, and

amplitude. Debug any distortion or noise issues. Document your design decisions and test

results.

Bonus: Add MIDI input so the synthesizer can be played from a keyboard or DAW.

This transforms it from a demo project into a genuinely usable instrument and shows

digital communication protocol knowledge.

@1nska  •  6 EE Portfolio Projects  •  Page 9

#4

MPPT Solar Charge Controller

POWER ELECTRONICS • RENEWABLE ENERGY • CONTROL SYSTEMS

Why recruiters love this: Power electronics is one of the highest-demand EE specializations.

Building an MPPT controller shows you understand DC-DC conversion, control loops, and renewable

energy systems — all in one project.

Build a Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) solar charge controller that optimizes energy harvest

from a solar panel and efficiently charges a battery. Unlike simple PWM controllers, MPPT

dynamically adjusts the operating point to extract maximum power regardless of conditions.

What you need:

• Small solar panel (10-20W)

• Arduino or STM32 microcontroller

• Buck or buck-boost converter components (MOSFET, inductor, diode, capacitors)

• INA219 current/voltage sensor module

• 12V lead-acid or lithium battery

• LCD display for status readout

Skills it proves:

• DC-DC converter design and analysis

• Control system implementation (Perturb & Observe algorithm)

• Power MOSFET driving and gate driver circuits

• Efficiency measurement and optimization

• Real-world renewable energy system understanding

How to build it:

Step 1: Build the buck converter. Design and assemble a basic DC-DC buck converter on a

breadboard. Use a MOSFET, Schottky diode, and inductor. Verify voltage step-down with a

bench power supply before connecting the solar panel.

Step 2: Add sensing. Wire INA219 modules to measure both the solar panel voltage/current and

the battery voltage/current. Log these values to verify your measurements are accurate.

@1nska  •  6 EE Portfolio Projects  •  Page 10

Step 3: Implement MPPT algorithm. Code the Perturb & Observe algorithm — slightly adjust the

duty cycle, measure if power increased or decreased, and continue in the direction that increases

power. This is the core of the project.

Step 4: Add battery management. Implement charging stages — bulk, absorption, float. Add

overvoltage and overcurrent protection in software. Add a physical fuse as a safety backup.

Step 5: Build the display interface. Show solar power in, battery voltage, charging current, and

efficiency on an LCD. Log data to an SD card for performance analysis over time.

Step 6: Test under real conditions. Take it outside, connect to a real solar panel, and charge a

real battery. Measure and document your MPPT efficiency vs. a simple direct-connect setup.

Bonus: Add WiFi connectivity and log performance data to a cloud dashboard.

Compare your MPPT efficiency across different weather conditions and times of day.

This data-driven approach impresses power systems employers.

@1nska  •  6 EE Portfolio Projects  •  Page 11

#5

Software-Defined Radio Receiver

RF • SIGNAL PROCESSING • COMMUNICATIONS

Why recruiters love this: RF and communications engineering is a specialized, high-paying niche.

Building an SDR receiver proves you understand the full signal chain — from antenna to

demodulated audio — and can work with real-world RF signals.

Build a software-defined radio that can receive and demodulate FM radio, aircraft communications

(ADS-B), weather satellite images, and more. You'll process raw RF data in software, implementing

filters, demodulators, and decoders that traditionally require expensive dedicated hardware.

What you need:

• RTL-SDR dongle (RTL2832U-based, ~$25)

• Antenna (dipole for FM, or build a QFH antenna for weather satellites)

• Python with NumPy, SciPy, and matplotlib

• GNU Radio (free, open-source SDR framework)

• Computer with USB port

• Optional: LNA (low noise amplifier) for weak signals

Skills it proves:

• RF fundamentals — frequency, bandwidth, modulation schemes

• Digital signal processing — FFT, filtering, sampling theory

• Communication protocols and demodulation techniques

• Python for real-time signal processing

• Antenna design basics

How to build it:

Step 1: Set up the RTL-SDR. Install drivers and GNU Radio. Verify you can receive FM radio —

tune to a local station and confirm you hear audio. This validates your entire receive chain.

Step 2: Build an FM demodulator from scratch. Using Python and NumPy, read raw IQ samples

from the RTL-SDR and implement FM demodulation manually — without GNU Radio blocks. This

proves you understand the DSP, not just the tools.

@1nska  •  6 EE Portfolio Projects  •  Page 12

Step 3: Visualize the spectrum. Build a real-time spectrum analyzer using FFT. Display a

waterfall plot showing signal activity across a frequency range. This is a powerful demo piece.

Step 4: Decode ADS-B aircraft signals. Tune to 1090 MHz and decode aircraft position and

identification data. Parse the binary protocol and plot aircraft positions on a map.

Step 5: Receive a weather satellite image. Build or buy a QFH antenna, receive a NOAA satellite

pass at 137 MHz, and decode the APT signal into an actual weather image. This is the

showstopper demo.

Step 6: Document everything. Create a GitHub repo with your Python code, GNU Radio

flowgraphs, antenna design, and example outputs (spectrum plots, decoded images, aircraft

tracks).

Bonus: Implement your own digital modulation scheme (BPSK or QPSK) and

transmit/receive data between two SDRs. Note: only transmit at legal power levels or

use a direct cable connection to stay compliant with regulations.

@1nska  •  6 EE Portfolio Projects  •  Page 13

#6

PID-Controlled Balancing Robot

CONTROL SYSTEMS • ROBOTICS • EMBEDDED

Why recruiters love this: Control systems are fundamental to EE and notoriously hard to implement

well in practice. A self-balancing robot is the perfect proof that you can tune a real control loop — not

just solve transfer functions on paper.

Build a two-wheeled robot that balances itself upright using a PID control loop. An IMU

(accelerometer + gyroscope) measures tilt angle, a microcontroller runs the PID algorithm, and DC

motors with encoders make corrections in real time. It's the inverted pendulum problem — brought to

life.

What you need:

• Arduino Mega or ESP32

• MPU6050 IMU (accelerometer + gyroscope)

• 2x DC gear motors with encoders

• L298N or TB6612FNG motor driver

• Robot chassis (3D print or use a kit frame)

• LiPo battery (7.4V 2S)

• Wheels with rubber tires for grip

Skills it proves:

• PID control theory and real-world tuning

• Sensor fusion (complementary or Kalman filter)

• Real-time embedded control with tight loop timing

• Motor control and H-bridge driver circuits

• System dynamics and stability analysis

How to build it:

Step 1: Get IMU data. Wire the MPU6050 to your Arduino, read raw accelerometer and

gyroscope values. Implement a complementary filter to fuse both sensors into a stable tilt angle

estimate.

@1nska  •  6 EE Portfolio Projects  •  Page 14

Step 2: Build the chassis. Mount the motors, wheels, battery, and electronics. Keep the center of

gravity high — this actually makes balancing easier (longer pendulum = slower fall). Ensure the

IMU is mounted at the pivot point.

Step 3: Implement basic PID. Start with proportional control only (P). Set I and D to zero.

Gradually increase P until the robot starts reacting to tilts. It will oscillate — that's expected.

Step 4: Tune the full PID loop. Add derivative (D) to dampen oscillations. Add integral (I) to

eliminate steady-state lean. Use the Ziegler-Nichols method or manual tuning. This is where you

really learn control systems.

Step 5: Add encoder feedback. Use motor encoders to implement a position hold — so the robot

doesn't just balance but stays in one place. This is a cascaded control loop (inner: balance, outer:

position).

Step 6: Demonstrate and document. Film the robot balancing, recovering from pushes, and

holding position. Show your PID tuning process and control system block diagram on GitHub.

Include plots of angle vs. time during tuning.

Bonus: Add Bluetooth or WiFi remote control so you can drive the robot while it

self-balances. Or implement LQR (Linear Quadratic Regulator) control instead of PID

and compare performance — this shows advanced control theory knowledge.

@1nska  •  6 EE Portfolio Projects  •  Page 15

What To Do Next

Don't try to build all 6 at once. Pick the one that excites you most, order the parts today, and start this

weekend. A finished project beats a perfect plan every time.

When you finish a project, document it properly: clean code on GitHub, a detailed README with

photos and diagrams, and a short demo video. That package is what gets you interviews.

If you want more guides like this — on building startups, career strategy for engineers, or bridging

business and engineering — follow me on Instagram. I'm documenting the entire journey.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Every radio transmission can be intercepted, direction-found, and jammed. Laser communication

eliminates all three problems: the beam is directional (impossible to intercept from the side), invisible

(808nm IR), and carries no RF signature. Military Special Operations, submarine-to-satellite links, and

inter-spacecraft communication all use optical links for exactly these reasons. This project builds a

complete encrypted optical link: modulated laser transmitter, avalanche photodiode receiver, clock

recovery, and AES encryption.

System Architecture

@1nska  •  Defense Tech Part 2: Laser + Covert Systems  •  Page 7

Encrypted data over invisible IR beam — no RF emission, cannot be intercepted

Cost: ~$12

Difficulty:
Intermediate-Advanced
Build Time: 1-2 weekends | • Transmitter — laser driver with OOK modulation: An 808nm laser diode driven by a MOSFET

switching circuit. On-Off Keying (OOK): laser on = 1, laser off = 0. The MCU (ESP32) encrypts the

data with AES-128, adds start/stop framing and Manchester en
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• Transmitter — laser driver with OOK modulation: An 808nm laser diode driven by a MOSFET

switching circuit. On-Off Keying (OOK): laser on = 1, laser off = 0. The MCU (ESP32) encrypts the

data with AES-128, adds start/stop framing and Manchester encoding (for clock recovery), then

drives the MOSFET at up to 1 Mbps.

• Receiver — avalanche photodiode (APD): An APD (or high-speed PIN diode like SFH213)

provides internal gain through avalanche multiplication. This gives 10-50x better sensitivity than a

standard photodiode. Biased at just below breakdown voltage (typically 100-150V from a boost

converter). The received photocurrent feeds a transimpedance amplifier.

• Clock recovery: Manchester encoding ensures a transition in every bit period, allowing the

receiver's PLL to synchronize its clock to the transmitter's bit rate. Without clock recovery, timing

drift over long messages causes bit errors. A simple DPLL (digital PLL) implemented on the

ESP32 handles this.

• AES decryption: The receiver ESP32 strips framing, decodes Manchester, and decrypts

AES-128 using a pre-shared key stored in flash. Output: original plaintext on serial terminal or

OLED display.

@1nska  •  Defense Tech Part 2: Laser + Covert Systems  •  Page 8

// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Spin a motor either direction at any speed you choose — the front end of every robot

## why this matters

Before a robot can balance, drive, or steer, something has to turn a control signal into
torque. An H-bridge does exactly that: four switches that push current through a DC motor in
either direction, plus PWM that sets how hard. Build one, drive a motor forward and reverse,
ramp its speed smoothly, and sense the current it draws, and you have the power stage that
sits under every motor-control project in this guide. It is the cheapest, most fundamental
motor build, and the payoff is immediate — a motor that does exactly what your code says.

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Seriously. The engineers who read docs outperform the ones who watch tutorials every single time.

Tutorials teach you to follow instructions. Documentation teaches you to think.

Why docs beat tutorials:

• Docs are written by the people who built the thing — tutorials are written by people who learned to

use it

• Docs are comprehensive — tutorials cherry-pick the easy parts

• Reading docs builds the skill of learning from primary sources — the #1 skill of senior engineers

• In interviews, saying "I read the RFC" signals a completely different level of seriousness

Docs to start with:

• Whatever framework you use daily — read it cover to cover, not just "Getting Started"

• MDN Web Docs — the bible for anything web-related

• Apple Developer Documentation — if you're building iOS/macOS

• Python official docs — especially the tutorial and library reference

• RFCs and specs — HTTP, TCP/IP, OAuth. Dense but incredibly rewarding

The habit:

Spend 20 minutes a day reading documentation instead of watching a tutorial. In 3 months, you'll

understand systems at a level most students don't reach in 4 years.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Every military targeting system, every autonomous vehicle LIDAR, every surveying instrument uses

laser time-of-flight ranging. The principle is simple: fire a short laser pulse, start a timer, stop it when

the reflection arrives, calculate distance from the round-trip time. The implementation is one of the

hardest analog design challenges in EE: generating nanosecond pulses, building a time-to-digital

converter with picosecond resolution, and designing a receiver sensitive enough to detect photons

reflected from hundreds of meters away.

Why this is the ultimate portfolio project: A working laser rangefinder

demonstrates high-speed analog design, precision timing circuits, optical

engineering, and signal processing — all in one device. It's the project that makes

interviewers stop asking standard questions and start having a technical

conversation.

System Architecture

@1nska  •  Defense Tech Part 2: Laser + Covert Systems  •  Page 10
canonicalDescription.summary:
Laser Rangefinder

Time-of-flight distance measurement with 5ns pulse and 100ps timing resolution | • Pulse generator (5ns): A MOSFET avalanche pulser circuit. A high-voltage supply (100-200V)

charges a small capacitor through a resistor. When the MOSFET is triggered, the cap discharges

through the laser diode in nanoseconds. The avalanche breakd
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• Pulse generator (5ns): A MOSFET avalanche pulser circuit. A high-voltage supply (100-200V)

charges a small capacitor through a resistor. When the MOSFET is triggered, the cap discharges

through the laser diode in nanoseconds. The avalanche breakdown of the MOSFET provides the

fast switching edge. Pulse width is determined by the capacitance and parasitic inductance —

keep leads short.

• Laser diode (905nm): A pulsed laser diode rated for high peak power (10-75W) but low average

power (duty cycle <0.1%). 905nm is standard for rangefinders because it's eye-safe at the power

levels used and atmospheric absorption is low. A collimating lens focuses the beam to <1 mrad

divergence.

• Receiver (APD): An avalanche photodiode with a narrowband 905nm filter and focusing optics.

The APD provides internal gain (x50-200) at a reverse bias of 100-200V. A transimpedance

amplifier converts the photocurrent pulse to a voltage pulse. A comparator with adjustable

threshold generates the STOP signal for the TDC.

• Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC): The heart of the system. The laser trigger pulse is the START

signal. The APD comparator output is the STOP signal. The TDC measures the time between

them. A TDC7200 IC provides 55ps resolution. Alternatively, build a Vernier delay line TDC from

discrete logic — two ring oscillators at slightly different frequencies that achieve interpolated timing

down to ~100ps.

• Distance calculation: Distance = (time × c) / 2, where c = 3×10I m/s. At 100ps resolution:

distance resolution = (100ps × 3×10I) / 2 = 1.5 cm. Average multiple measurements to reduce

noise and improve resolution further.

@1nska  •  Defense Tech Part 2: Laser + Covert Systems  •  Page 11

The modern border and base perimeter is watched by autonomous sensor towers: they detect motion,

classify what it is, slew a camera to track it, and alert an operator — no human staring at a

screen. Build a small one: a pan-tilt camera head on a mast, a wide-field motion trigger, a person

/ vehicle classifier, a tracking loop that keeps the target centred, and an alert with a snapshot

to your phone (or your command map in project 6). Watch it wake up, turn, and follow you across

the yard. It is perception, control, and systems integration — and, because it only watches,

entirely a sensor.

Sweeping the spectrum: An SDR retunes across the bands in steps, capturing a power spectrum at

each; stitched together it is a wideband survey. Repeated continuously, it becomes a time-lapse

of the radio environment.

▸

Baseline and change detection: Log the average power per frequency over days to build a

baseline; a signal where the baseline is empty is a new emitter. Flagging those is the

station’s alert function — spectrum change detection.

▸

Decoding the public: Dedicated decoders turn broadcasts into data: ADS-B (aircraft positions),

AIS (ships), NOAA / Meteor weather images, FM and DAB. Each becomes a feed on your map.

▸

The station: A fixed mast antenna (a discone for wideband, plus dedicated antennas), low-loss

coax, an LNA, and an SDR into a Pi running always-on software — with a waterfall dashboard you

can open from any device.

▸

Feeding the picture: Every decoded track and every emitter alert is published to the command

map (project 6), so it shows aircraft, ships, and radio activity live around you.

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
Most knobs are passive; this one fights back. By driving a brushless motor with FOC and
reading its exact angle, you can render torque as a function of position — so the same
physical knob can feel like clicky detents, a smooth spring that returns to centre, or a hard
end-stop, all changed in software. It is the technology behind high-end car controls and the
viral “smart knob,” and it is a brilliant lesson in torque control and haptics: you are
programming a force field you can feel with your fingers. It builds directly on FOC and turns
motor control into a user interface.

import cv2

picam2 = Picamera2()

})

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")

    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)

    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break
