canonicalDescription.purpose:
Every WiFi and Bluetooth chip has a unique RF signature caused by manufacturing variations —

slightly different oscillator frequencies, amplifier gain curves, and phase noise profiles. MAC addresses

can be spoofed in software. RF fingerprints cannot — they're determined by the physics of the silicon.

This project builds an RF front end that captures these signatures and matches them against known

devices. This is active research at DARPA and is used in military IFF (Identification Friend or Foe)

systems.

System Architecture
canonicalDescription.summary:
RF Fingerprinting Authenticator

Identify wireless devices by their unique manufacturing imperfections | • 2.4GHz antenna: A PCB patch antenna or quarter-wave monopole tuned to 2.4GHz. Captures

WiFi/BT preamble transmissions from nearby devices.

• LNA + Mixer: SPF5189Z amplifies the signal. A mixer (with local oscillator from Si5351 clock

generator)
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• 2.4GHz antenna: A PCB patch antenna or quarter-wave monopole tuned to 2.4GHz. Captures

WiFi/BT preamble transmissions from nearby devices.

• LNA + Mixer: SPF5189Z amplifies the signal. A mixer (with local oscillator from Si5351 clock

generator) downconverts to an intermediate frequency suitable for SDR sampling.

• I/Q demodulator: Extracts in-phase and quadrature components of the signal. This preserves

both amplitude AND phase information — the phase is where manufacturing differences are most

@1nska  •  6 AI-Era EE Projects  •  Page 18

visible.

• Dual ADC: Two channels sample I and Q simultaneously. ADS1115 for slow capture or

RTL-SDR for high-speed. The key is capturing the first few microseconds of a transmission

preamble, where the oscillator startup transient reveals the device's unique signature.

• Correlator: Python or FPGA-based correlation engine compares captured preamble IQ data

against a database of known device signatures. Uses cross-correlation peak and phase offset as

matching criteria.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
During the Cold War, intelligence agencies developed laser listening devices that could extract audio

from vibrating surfaces at distance. The principle is simple: sound waves inside a room cause the

window glass to vibrate by nanometers. An IR laser bouncing off that window is phase-modulated by

the vibration. A sensitive photodetector reads that modulation, and an FM demodulator extracts the

audio. The technique was declassified decades ago, but the analog design challenges remain:

sub-millivolt signal detection, laser intensity stabilization, and FM demodulation of an extremely weak

carrier.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand optical signal chains, laser driver

design, transimpedance amplification at the noise floor, and analog FM

demodulation. These skills directly apply to LIDAR, fiber optics, optical sensing, and

defense.

System Architecture

@1nska  •  Defense Tech Part 2: Laser + Covert Systems  •  Page 3
canonicalDescription.summary:
Laser Surveillance Microphone

Hear through a window from 100m — no mic in the room, no RF, no trace | • IR laser diode (808nm): A collimated infrared laser aimed at a window pane. The laser must be

intensity-stabilized using an APC (automatic power control) circuit — a monitor photodiode inside

the laser package feeds back to the driver, keeping ou
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• IR laser diode (808nm): A collimated infrared laser aimed at a window pane. The laser must be

intensity-stabilized using an APC (automatic power control) circuit — a monitor photodiode inside

the laser package feeds back to the driver, keeping output power constant. Any intensity drift

appears as noise in the received signal.

• Window vibration: Sound waves inside the room cause the glass to vibrate. A normal

conversation at 60dB SPL causes ~1-10nm of displacement on a window pane. This displacement

phase-modulates the reflected laser beam — the path length changes by twice the displacement

(there and back), creating a Doppler shift proportional to the velocity of the glass surface.

• Photodetector + TIA: A large-area silicon photodiode (BPW34 or similar) with a transimpedance

amplifier (1MΩ feedback) captures the reflected beam. The DC component represents the average

reflected power. The AC component (microvolts) carries the audio information. A coupling

capacitor separates them.

• Bandpass filter (300Hz-3kHz): A 4th-order Sallen-Key bandpass isolates the speech band. This

removes laser noise below 300Hz and high-frequency detector noise above 3kHz.

• FM demodulator: The phase modulation from the window vibration is equivalent to FM. A simple

PLL-based FM demodulator (LM567 or NE567) or a slope detector (tuned LC circuit on the slope

of the resonance curve) extracts the audio. Amplify and output to speaker or ADC.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
In electronic warfare, the three threats to radio communication are: interception (listening), direction

finding (locating the transmitter), and jamming (disrupting the signal). A burst transmitter defeats all

three. The message is compressed and encrypted, then transmitted in a single 50ms burst on a

pseudo-random frequency. 50ms is too short for most direction-finding systems to get a bearing.

Frequency hopping means a jammer doesn't know which frequency to block. AES encryption means

even if the burst is recorded, it can't be read. This is the fundamental operating principle of military

SINCGARS and HAVE QUICK radios.

System Architecture

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• Message input: User types a text message on the ESP32 serial terminal (up to 256 characters).

The MCU compresses the text using run-length encoding (saves ~30% on typical messages) and

encrypts with AES-256 using a pre-shared key.

• FHSS sequence generation: A pseudo-random number generator (seeded with a shared

secret) generates a sequence of frequencies across the ISM band (902-928 MHz for US, or 433

MHz band). The TX and RX use the same seed, so they hop to the same frequencies at the same

time.

• Si4432 RF module: A frequency-agile transceiver that can retune in <100µs. The MCU sends

the encrypted, compressed packet in a single 50ms burst. During the burst, the frequency hops

every 5ms across 10 channels. Total airtime per channel: 5ms — below the threshold of most

spectrum analyzers and DF systems.

• Receiver: An identical Si4432 + ESP32 module, time-synchronized with the transmitter (either

GPS-disciplined clocks or a pre-agreed hop schedule). The receiver hops through the same

frequency sequence, collecting 5ms fragments and reassembling the full packet. Decrypt and

display.

DO THIS
Upload the Blink example, then change the delay from 1000 ms to 100 ms and watch it

THE TRAP
Copy-pasting a whole project on day two. Every build here is under 15 lines — type
them, break them, fix them.

You can make the LED, the buzzer and the button work together without looking
anything up.

STEP 03
Now learn the theory you just used.

DO THIS
You've already used Ohm's law (that 220 ohm resistor), Kirchhoff's laws (the current
through your LED loop) and a pull-up resistor. Go back and read exactly those: V =
IR, series vs parallel, voltage dividers, why the LED needs a resistor at all. The

concepts stick because you've held the parts.

Trying to finish a 900-page textbook before touching a wire. Read one chapter, build

one thing, repeat.

You can calculate the resistor for any LED from its datasheet and explain why 5 V

straight into an LED kills it.

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• The scintillator: A block of plastic scintillator (cast PVT, or a surplus offcut) emits a brief flash of blue
light when a charged particle deposits energy crossing it. A single muon produces only a few
hundred to a few thousand photons — faint and fast, lasting nanoseconds.

• Silicon photomultiplier (SiPM): A SiPM is an array of avalanche photodiodes biased just above
breakdown, giving enormous gain (around 106) — enough to turn a handful of photons into a
measurable current pulse. It replaces the bulky, high-voltage photomultiplier tubes of old with a 6
mm chip running on about 29 V.

• Precise bias + temperature: A SiPM's gain is steeply sensitive to bias voltage and temperature, so a
stable, low-noise bias supply (a quiet boost converter plus filtering) is critical. Drift the voltage and
your count rate drifts with it — which is why real systems add temperature compensation.

• Fast amplifier: A transimpedance or voltage amplifier with enough bandwidth (tens of MHz) converts
the SiPM's fast current spike into a clean voltage pulse without smearing it. Layout matters here —
short traces, good grounding, and supply bypassing keep noise below the tiny signal.

• Discrimination and counting: A comparator fires when a pulse exceeds a threshold set just above
the noise floor, producing a clean digital tick per event. An MCU counts ticks and shows the muon
rate on an OLED. Add a second detector and require coincidence — only count when both fire at
once — to reject electrical noise and confirm real through-going particles.

@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Reach Space   •   Page 20

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Watch your own heartbeat draw itself on screen, wave by wave

## why this matters

Every beat of your heart is a coordinated electrical wave, and it is large enough to read
from your skin. Put two electrodes across your chest or arms, run them into a biopotential
front end, and the classic PQRST complex appears on screen: the small P wave as the atria
fire, the sharp QRS spike as the ventricles contract, the broad T wave as they reset. Then
detect those R peaks and you have a live heart rate and beat-to-beat variability. It is the
most iconic biosignal there is, the payoff is unmistakable, and it is the project that proves
you can build precision analog that works on a living system.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Radar cross-section (RCS) is the measure of how visible an object is to radar. A large RCS means

easy to detect; a small RCS means stealthy. Every stealth aircraft, ship, and vehicle is designed to

minimize RCS through shape (angling surfaces away from the radar) and materials (absorbing radar

energy instead of reflecting it). This project builds a bistatic RCS measurement system using two

HB100 modules — one as transmitter, one as receiver — that lets you measure RCS reduction of

different shapes and coatings at 10.5 GHz. You're doing what Lockheed does in anechoic chambers,

on your desk.

import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Software safety mechanisms can be overridden by software. A hardware kill switch cannot. This project

monitors the real-time power draw pattern of an AI compute board (Jetson Nano, Coral TPU, etc.) and

compares it against expected inference signatures. If the power pattern deviates beyond a threshold —

suggesting unexpected computation — a relay physically cuts the power rail. No firmware can override

a relay that has already opened the circuit.

System Architecture
canonicalDescription.summary:
Hardware AI Kill Switch

Analog watchdog that physically disconnects AI hardware when power signature

deviates | • Current sense resistor: A 10mΩ shunt resistor in series with the AI board's power rail. Produces

a small voltage proportional to current draw. At 3A peak: 30mV full scale.

• Differential amplifier + filter: INA219 or discrete diff-amp (gain of 10
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• Current sense resistor: A 10mΩ shunt resistor in series with the AI board's power rail. Produces

a small voltage proportional to current draw. At 3A peak: 30mV full scale.

• Differential amplifier + filter: INA219 or discrete diff-amp (gain of 100) amplifies the shunt

voltage. A low-pass filter at 100Hz smooths high-frequency switching noise while preserving the

inference power envelope.

@1nska  •  6 AI-Era EE Projects  •  Page 9

• ADC (ADS1115): 16-bit ADC samples the amplified signal at 860 SPS. Gives 1ms resolution of

the power waveform — enough to capture inference cycles.

• MCU pattern matching: An ATmega328 or ESP32 compares the real-time power waveform

against a stored 'expected' template using cross-correlation. If correlation drops below threshold

for >500ms, it triggers the relay.

• Relay driver: A logic-level MOSFET (IRLZ44N) drives a 10A automotive relay. Normally closed

— power flows to AI board. On trigger, MOSFET turns off, relay opens, power rail is physically cut.

A manual reset button is required to reconnect.

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Read a surface's vibration with a reflected beam — non-contact sensing with light

## why this matters

Point a laser at a reflective surface, catch the reflected dot on a photodiode, and any
vibration of that surface changes the light reaching your detector — letting you read the
surface’s motion without touching it. This is laser vibrometry, a real engineering technique
for measuring how speakers, motors, and structures vibrate without loading them down.
Building one teaches optical detection of tiny displacements, signal recovery from a noisy
photodetector, and the limits of non-contact sensing. It is one of the most striking
demonstrations of how much information a single beam of light carries.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
A satellite in orbit has no ground to push against, so how does it turn to point a camera or antenna?
Most spacecraft use reaction wheels: spin a flywheel one way and conservation of angular momentum
rotates the spacecraft the other way. Speed the wheel up or slow it down and you apply precise torque
to the body — no fuel, no thrusters. This project builds a single-axis reaction-wheel platform (or the
dramatic reaction-wheel pendulum that balances on an edge): an IMU senses the platform's angle, a
control loop computes the torque needed, and a motor accelerates a flywheel to deliver it. It is the
cleanest possible demonstration of real attitude control — the same principle flying on every imaging
satellite, the Hubble Space Telescope, and the control gyros of the ISS.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand closed-loop control (PID/LQR), sensor fusion,
BLDC motor torque control, and real-time embedded firmware. Attitude determination and control is
a core aerospace discipline, and the same fundamentals underpin robotics, drones, and
self-balancing vehicles.

@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Reach Space   •   Page 10
canonicalDescription.summary:
A spinning flywheel rotates and holds a platform's heading — how satellites point
without thrusters | • Conservation of angular momentum: The platform sits on a low-friction bearing. When the motor
accelerates the flywheel clockwise, the platform reacts by rotating counter-clockwise. The torque on
the body equals the rate of change of the wheel's ang
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• Conservation of angular momentum: The platform sits on a low-friction bearing. When the motor
accelerates the flywheel clockwise, the platform reacts by rotating counter-clockwise. The torque on
the body equals the rate of change of the wheel's angular momentum — so wheel acceleration is
your control input.

• IMU attitude sensing: An MPU-6050 or BNO055 IMU fuses its gyroscope and accelerometer to
estimate the platform's tilt angle and angular rate. A complementary or Kalman filter blends the
drift-free-but-noisy accelerometer with the smooth-but-drifting gyro.

• The control loop: A PID (or LQR) controller takes the angle error and computes a commanded
wheel torque. For the balancing-pendulum version it must stabilize an inherently unstable
equilibrium — like balancing a broom on your palm, but a thousand times a second.

• BLDC torque control: A brushless gimbal motor spins the flywheel. A field-oriented control (FOC)
driver regulates motor current, and since torque is proportional to current, this gives direct, smooth
torque control — far better than crude PWM speed control.

• Momentum saturation: If the platform keeps disturbing in one direction, the wheel spins faster and
faster until it hits its limit — saturation. Real satellites dump this momentum with magnetorquers or
thrusters. On the bench you will watch the wheel max out and learn why momentum management
matters.

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
This is the single most important step in this entire guide. I convinced KUKA — one of the world's top

robotics companies — to let me borrow a robot for an art engineering performance. No budget. No

connections. No one handed it to me. I just reached out, pitched the vision, and made it happen. That one

project taught me more than any class and gave me something concrete to talk about in every

conversation.

Why this works:

• It proves initiative — anyone can do homework, very few people build on their own

• It creates real stories for interviews ("Tell me about a project...")

• You learn 10x faster when you're solving real problems, not textbook exercises

• It gives you something to put on your resume that isn't a class project everyone else also has

What to build (start here):

• Solve your own problem: What annoys you? What's inefficient? Build a tool to fix it

• Pitch something bold: Reach out to companies, labs, or people way above your level. The worst

they can say is no

• Clone and improve: Rebuild a product you use daily, then add a feature they don't have

• Automate something: Find a manual process and engineer it away

The bar:

Your project should be something you can demo in 60 seconds and explain why it matters in one

sentence. It doesn't need to be perfect. It needs to be shipped.

I Ship > perfect. A finished ugly app beats an unfinished beautiful one every time.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
A robot arm looks simple until you try to move its hand to a specific point in space: you have to solve, in reverse, what every

joint angle must be to put the gripper there. That is inverse kinematics, and it is the difference between a servo puppet and

a robot you command in coordinates. Build a 4-axis arm, derive its geometry, implement IK, and you can type a position and
watch it reach there, then pick up an object and place it somewhere else. It is the classic centrepiece of robotics, the

flagship of this guide, and a direct lesson in the math every industrial arm runs.
canonicalDescription.summary:
Tell the arm an X, Y, Z and it works out every joint angle itself — pick and place, from math | BUILD NOTE

Print a proven open-source quadruped frame rather than designing your own, use decent metal-gear servos (cheap

plastic ones strip under load), and power the servos from a dedicated high-current supply. Get one leg’s IK working

standing
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
BUILD NOTE

Print a proven open-source quadruped frame rather than designing your own, use decent metal-gear servos (cheap

plastic ones strip under load), and power the servos from a dedicated high-current supply. Get one leg’s IK working

standing still before you attempt a single step.

Legs are arms: Each leg has three joints — hip abduction, hip pitch, knee — and placing a foot at an (x, y, z) is the same

inverse-kinematics problem as the arm, solved twelve times over for four legs.

▸

Gaits: A gait is the pattern of which legs are in the air and which are on the ground. A creep moves one leg at a time

(slow, always stable); a trot moves diagonal pairs together (faster, needs balance). Phasing the legs correctly is what

makes walking work.

▸

Stability: When a leg lifts, the body must stay balanced over the remaining feet. The support polygon — the area under

the grounded feet — must contain the centre of mass, or the robot tips. Shifting the body before lifting a leg is the trick.

▸

Swing and stance: A stepping leg swings forward through the air; the grounded legs stroke backward together to push

the body forward. Coordinating swing and stance across all legs, cycle after cycle, is the gait engine.

▸

Torque and timing: Twelve servos moving under load draw serious current and must move smoothly and in sync. A
dedicated supply, sensible speeds, and a fixed-rate control loop are the difference between a walk and a twitching heap.
▸

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Out in orbit there is nothing to push against, so spacecraft change and hold their orientation by firing
small thrusters — the reaction control system (RCS). You can build the same thing on the ground:
mount a platform on a near-frictionless bearing, plumb a few small solenoid valves to a
compressed-gas supply, and fire short puffs to rotate it and hold a commanded heading. An IMU
senses the angle, a controller decides which thruster to pulse and for how long, and the platform slews
and stops on target — no wheels, no contact, just gas. This is exactly how satellites maneuver, and the
air-bearing version is literally how aerospace labs test real attitude-control hardware before flight. It is
the most viscerally 'spacecraft' project you can build on a bench.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand reaction-control propulsion, closed-loop attitude
control, solenoid valve driving and pulse-width thrust modulation, and inertial sensing. Propulsion
and GNC are core spacecraft disciplines, and demonstrating thruster-based attitude control on an air
bearing is exactly the kind of hardware aerospace teams build and test.

→ The job this maps to: spacecraft propulsion and GNC — satellite and launch companies, and the
air-bearing test labs that validate attitude-control systems.

Safety: Compressed gas is genuinely dangerous. Use only a properly rated regulator and tubing,
never exceed component pressure ratings, and secure the gas supply so it cannot become a
projectile. Use inert gas (CO2 or filtered compressed air) — never anything flammable or an
unregulated high-pressure source — wear eye protection, and fully depressurize before working on
the plumbing.

A platform that rotates and holds its heading by firing puffs of compressed gas —
exactly like a spacecraft's RCS | • Newton's third law in a vacuum: A spacecraft cannot push against anything, so it carries its own

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• Newton's third law in a vacuum: A spacecraft cannot push against anything, so it carries its own
reaction mass: expel gas one way, the body rotates the other. Firing a thruster offset from the
center of mass produces a torque that slews the vehicle. Your bench version does the identical
thing on a low-friction bearing that mimics the freedom of orbit.

• Near-frictionless bearing: The platform sits on a ball bearing, a lazy-Susan, or — for the stretch
version — a planar air bearing that floats it on a thin film of air. The lower the friction, the more the
demo behaves like a real satellite, where the only torques are the ones you command.

• Solenoid 'thrusters': Small 12 V solenoid valves act as on/off thrusters. Mounted in opposing pairs
at the platform's edge and fed from a regulated gas line, each releases a puff of gas through a
nozzle when energized. Opposing pairs let you torque clockwise or counter-clockwise.

• Pulsed thrust control: You cannot throttle a solenoid, so you modulate thrust the way real RCS does
— by pulse width and pulse frequency. Short pulses give fine control near the target; longer or more
frequent pulses give a fast slew. The controller translates a commanded torque into a valve on-time.

• Closed-loop attitude control: An IMU measures the platform's angle and rate; a PD controller
computes the torque needed to reach and hold the setpoint, then thruster-selection logic fires the
correct valve. Because gas is limited, the controller must avoid a 'limit cycle' — chattering around
the target and wasting gas — which is a real spacecraft design problem.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Outdoors, GPS tells the flight controller where the drone is. Indoors there is no GPS, and a drone drifts like a balloon in a draft.

The fix is the same trick an optical mouse uses: a tiny downward camera (a PMW3901 optical-flow sensor) watches the floor
texture slide by and reports velocity, while a rangefinder gives height. Feed both to the flight controller and it holds position —

a hover you can let go of, indoors, that stays put. It is the cheapest, most dramatic upgrade there is, and it is the foundation

for every kind of indoor autonomy.
canonicalDescription.summary:
Optical flow: The sensor sees floor texture move across its tiny image and reports pixel displacement per frame — the

angular rate of the ground beneath. It is a mouse sensor pointed at the floor from a metre up.

▸

Height turns flow into velocity:
canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Optical flow: The sensor sees floor texture move across its tiny image and reports pixel displacement per frame — the

angular rate of the ground beneath. It is a mouse sensor pointed at the floor from a metre up.

▸

Height turns flow into velocity: The same angular rate means a faster ground speed when you are higher, so the flight

controller needs the height from a rangefinder (a ToF like the VL53L1X or a TFmini) to scale flow into linear velocity.

▸

Fusion in the estimator: The flight controller’s EKF fuses flow velocity with the IMU and the rangefinder into a position
estimate whose drift is bounded by the flow — no GPS required. It also enables terrain-following altitude hold.
▸

Light and texture: Flow needs texture and light: a blank floor or a dim room starves it. A small downward LED and a
textured surface make the difference between a locked hover and a drift.
▸

Flight modes: With flow enabled, position-hold and loiter modes work indoors, and the controller arbitrates between GPS

and flow depending on what is healthy. Understanding that arbitration is what keeps a hybrid indoor / outdoor flight safe.

Getting supplies to a precise spot from the air is a logistics problem the defense world solved with self-steering parafoils: a

ram-air canopy with servo-pulled control lines and a GPS-guided controller that flies the payload to a coordinate. Build a
small one — a ram-air kite canopy, two servos on the brake lines, a GPS and IMU on the payload box — drop it from a legal

height, and watch it turn toward the landing point and flare. It is aerospace, control, and embedded engineering in one build,

it is pure cargo delivery, and it is one of the most satisfying autonomous systems you can make.

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
SP06 · 48.0 °C · ε 0.95

The environmental profiles: MIL-STD-810 defines test methods — high and low temperature, thermal shock, vibration,
mechanical shock, humidity, and more — each with a profile of levels and durations matched to the intended environment.
▸

The thermal chamber: An insulated box with a heater (and a Peltier or freezer for cold), a fan for uniformity, and a

thermocouple-controlled loop cycles the device between extremes and holds it there while it runs.

▸

The vibration table: A platform driven by an eccentric motor or a speaker reproduces transport vibration; an

accelerometer on the table confirms the levels and frequencies you are actually delivering.

▸

Shock and drop: A controlled drop from a set height onto a hard surface delivers a mechanical shock; an accelerometer

on the device records the peak g. Repeatable orientation and height are what make it a test rather than an accident.

▸

The device under test: The DUT runs a self-test loop and logs continuously, so you can see exactly when — and whether —
it faulted, reset, or failed during each profile. Pass / fail is defined before the test, not after.

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Stop measuring speed, start measuring distance — the principle inside adaptive cruise
control

## why this matters

Doppler tells you how fast something moves; FMCW (frequency-modulated continuous-wave) radar
tells you how far away it is. By sweeping the transmit frequency up in a linear “chirp,” the
returning echo is delayed — and because the transmitter has moved on in frequency during that
delay, mixing the two produces a beat whose frequency encodes range. This is the exact
technique inside automotive adaptive-cruise and weather radar, and building even a short-
range version is the leap from “I detected motion” to “I measured the scene.” It is the most
ambitious build here, so the trick is to build it module-based or as the classic coffee-can
radar rather than laying out microwave boards from scratch.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
To point itself, a spacecraft first has to know which way it is facing — and the simplest, cheapest,
most-flown way to get a reference is to find the Sun. A sun sensor measures the direction to the Sun in
the spacecraft's own frame, and that single vector is enough to constrain attitude for power-positioning
and coarse pointing. This project builds a real one: an arrangement of photodiodes (or a pinhole over a
small sensor array) whose relative readings encode the Sun's angle, plus the math to turn those
readings into a sun vector. It is a clean, satisfying sensor project — analog front end, geometry, and
calibration — and it is a genuine flight sensor, not a toy.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand optical attitude sensing, photodiode analog
front-ends and ratiometric measurement, the geometry of converting intensities into an angle, and
sensor calibration. Sun sensors fly on nearly every satellite, and building one is a recognizable
ADCS sensing skill.

→ The job this maps to: attitude determination (ADCS) — CubeSat and satellite companies, and
sensor/ADCS subsystem teams.

@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Build a Real Satellite   •   Page 17
canonicalDescription.summary:
A photodiode-array sensor that computes the exact direction to the Sun — the
most-flown attitude sensor in space | • Why the Sun: The Sun is a bright, effectively point source in a known direction, making it the easiest
celestial reference to measure. Knowing the sun vector in the body frame lets a spacecraft orient its
solar panels and perform coarse attitude co
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• Why the Sun: The Sun is a bright, effectively point source in a known direction, making it the easiest
celestial reference to measure. Knowing the sun vector in the body frame lets a spacecraft orient its
solar panels and perform coarse attitude control — which is why almost every satellite carries a sun
sensor.

• Photodiodes at angles: If you mount photodiodes facing slightly different directions (or put a single
pinhole/mask over a small array), each receives sunlight at a different incidence angle. Since a
photodiode's output falls off predictably with angle (roughly as the cosine), the relative outputs
depend on where the Sun is.

• Ratiometric measurement: Absolute brightness varies with distance and conditions, so you do not
use raw values — you use ratios between diodes. Ratios cancel overall intensity and depend only
on the angle, which is the trick that makes the sensor robust. This is the same principle as
commercial analog sun sensors.

• Analog front end: Each photodiode's tiny current is converted to a voltage by a transimpedance
amplifier and read by the MCU's ADC. Matching the channels and keeping noise low matters,
because the angle accuracy comes directly from how cleanly you measure the photocurrents.

• Computing the sun vector: From the calibrated ratios, the MCU computes the two angles that
define the Sun's direction (azimuth and elevation in the sensor frame), outputting a unit vector.
Calibrating against known Sun angles turns the raw geometry into an accurate sensor.

@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Build a Real Satellite   •   Page 18

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Ships continuously broadcast their identity, GPS position, course, speed, and cargo type on marine
VHF (161.975 and 162.025 MHz) using a system called AIS — the maritime equivalent of aircraft
ADS-B. It is unencrypted and required on most large vessels, so with an SDR tuned to the marine band
you can plot live ship traffic on a map: tankers, ferries, fishing boats, naval auxiliaries, each with its
name and destination. If you are anywhere near a coast, port, or large river, the result is a busy
real-time picture of maritime traffic — and the same volunteer-receiver model behind the public
ship-tracking sites.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand VHF reception, GMSK demodulation, the
AIS/NMEA message format, and multi-channel decoding. Receiving and plotting a live maritime
datalink is a concrete RF and decoding skill directly relevant to maritime, surveillance, and
wireless-systems work.

→ The job this maps to: maritime / navigation systems, coastal surveillance, and SDR/RF roles —
shipping, port authorities, defence, and tracking networks.

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• AIS on marine VHF: The Automatic Identification System broadcasts on two channels near 162
MHz. Vessels send their MMSI identity, GPS position, course, speed, and (in static messages) ship
name, type, and destination, on a self-organising time-division schedule so many ships share the
channel.

• Two channels at once: AIS uses 161.975 MHz (channel A) and 162.025 MHz (channel B). A
capable receiver decodes both simultaneously — the RTL-SDR's bandwidth easily spans both, and
the decoder splits and demodulates each.

• GMSK modulation: AIS uses Gaussian minimum-shift keying at 9600 bps — a compact,
constant-envelope FSK variant. The decoder demodulates GMSK, recovers the HDLC-framed
packets, and checks each with a CRC.

• NMEA decoding: Valid packets are turned into NMEA AIS sentences (the same format chartplotters
use). Software like AIS-catcher or rtl-ais parses these into position and vessel-info records.

• Plot the traffic: Feed the decoded positions to a map (AIS-catcher's web UI or a plotter). Ships
appear with names, headings, and tracks; static messages fill in type and destination. Near a coast
you will see a constantly updating maritime picture.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
A satellite lives and dies by its power system. The EPS (electrical power subsystem) harvests energy
from solar panels, charges and protects the battery, regulates it into the voltage rails every other
subsystem needs, and reports power health as telemetry — all of it autonomously, because there is no
one to flip a switch in orbit. This project builds a real one: a solar input stage that charges a lithium
battery safely, regulated output rails, protection against over-current and over-discharge, and
voltage/current telemetry on every channel. It is the same architecture as a flight EPS, and it is the
subsystem that keeps everything else alive — which is exactly why power engineers are always in
demand.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand solar energy harvesting, lithium battery charging
and protection, DC-DC regulation and power distribution, and power telemetry/monitoring. The EPS
is mission-critical on every spacecraft, and building one demonstrates real power-electronics and
systems competence.

→ The job this maps to: electrical power systems (EPS) — satellite and CubeSat companies, and
power-electronics subsystem teams.

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• Harvesting solar power: Solar cells are the only energy source in orbit, but their output swings with
sun angle and temperature. The charge stage (often with MPPT, as in the solar-controller project)
extracts as much power as conditions allow and uses it to charge the battery.

• Battery charging + protection: A lithium battery must be charged within strict voltage and current
limits and protected against over-charge, over-discharge, over-current, and temperature extremes
— any of which can damage or destroy it. The EPS enforces all of this automatically; in space there
is no replacing a cooked battery.

• Regulated distribution: Different subsystems need different, clean voltages (e.g. 3.3 V for logic, 5 V
for radios). DC-DC converters generate these regulated rails from the battery, and the EPS
distributes them — often with the ability to switch individual loads on and off.

• Protection and autonomy: Each rail has over-current protection so one faulty subsystem cannot pull
down the whole bus, and the battery has an under-voltage cutoff so the satellite can safely 'brown
out' and recover. This autonomy is essential — the spacecraft must protect itself.

• Power telemetry: The EPS measures voltage and current at the solar input, the battery, and each
rail, and reports them as telemetry. Operators watch this to understand the energy balance — is the
satellite generating more than it consumes? — one of the most important health metrics of any
mission.

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
Every drone company assumes a graduate has only ever flashed Betaflight, and that assumption
is usually correct. This project forces you through the part the firmware hides: raw gyro
rates and accelerometer vectors coming in at 1 kHz, a complementary (or Kalman) filter turning
them into a roll and pitch angle, and a PID loop turning that angle error into motor commands.
You will discover that the textbook loop oscillates on a real rig, that the gyro drifts, that
the accelerometer lies under vibration, and that the difference between a stable hover and a
flip is a derivative term and a 100 Hz low-pass filter. Debugging that on a hinged one-axis
test stand, with a logged plot of setpoint versus measured angle, is the actual skill a
flight-controls engineer is hired for.

// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Drive a brushless motor smoothly and silently — the technology in drones, EVs, and robot
dogs

## why this matters

Brushless (BLDC / PMSM) motors are everywhere high performance matters — drones, EVs, robot
joints, gimbals — because they are efficient, powerful, and long-lived. But they need
electronic commutation: you must energise the right coils at the right instant based on rotor
position. Field-Oriented Control (FOC) does this optimally, producing smooth, silent, full-
torque-at-any-speed motion, even holding still. Building a FOC drive — with a position
sensor, a three-phase driver, and a library like SimpleFOC — is the leap into modern motor
control and one of the most in-demand EE skills in robotics and electrified everything.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
AI assistants today are emotionally blind. They respond the same way whether you're calm, stressed,

or exhausted. This pendant adds a physiological context channel — fusing heart rate variability, skin

conductance, jaw tension, and voice prosody — to produce a continuous emotional state estimate that

the AI can use. Imagine ChatGPT knowing you're stressed before you ask for help. Or your AI calendar

refusing to schedule a meeting when you're fatigued. This is the missing input modality for human-AI

interaction.

System Architecture

Difficulty:

Build Time: 2-4 weekends | • Multi-modal sensor array: The pendant houses 4 sensor channels — 2 ECG electrodes for

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• Multi-modal sensor array: The pendant houses 4 sensor channels — 2 ECG electrodes for

heart rate variability (HRV), 2 GSR electrodes for skin conductance, 1 EMG channel for jaw

muscle tension, and a small MEMS microphone for voice prosody analysis.

• Sensor fusion processor: An STM32 runs 4 parallel signal processing chains. HRV: R-peak

detection from ECG, time-domain and frequency-domain HRV metrics. GSR: AC-excited

conductance measurement with synchronous demod. EMG: standard biosignal pipeline. Voice:

pitch tracking, formant extraction, prosody features.

• Emotion classifier (CNN+LSTM): A hybrid network that ingests all 4 feature streams. CNN

extracts local features per stream; LSTM models temporal dynamics; final dense layer classifies

into emotional states (calm, focused, stressed, fatigued, excited).

• Bluetooth output: The classified emotional state streams via BLE to a connected phone or AI

service. APIs can subscribe to emotion state changes and adapt their responses accordingly. The

OpenAI API, for example, could receive emotion as a system message context: 'User is currently

stressed and fatigued.'

// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

Every robot, from a vacuum to a Mars rover, runs the same loop: sense the world, decide what to do, act, repeat. A reactive

rover is the purest version — an ultrasonic and a pair of IR sensors feed a few simple rules that steer two motors, and the

machine roams a room avoiding walls and furniture with no map and no plan. It is the cheapest way to build something that
behaves on its own, the payoff is immediate (it just drives off), and it is the chassis and control skeleton every later project

in this guide builds on.

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
Forward kinematics: Given the joint angles and link lengths, trigonometry tells you where the gripper ends up. It is the

easy direction, and it is how you verify your model against the real arm.

▸

Inverse kinematics: Given a target (x, y, z), you solve backward for the joint angles. For a 4-axis arm: base rotation from

the target’s bearing, then a planar two-link triangle (shoulder and elbow) solved with the law of cosines, then the wrist

to level the gripper.

▸

The two-link triangle: The shoulder, elbow, and target form a triangle whose sides are your link lengths and the distance

to the target. The law of cosines gives the elbow angle; a little more trig gives the shoulder. That is the heart of the

solution.

▸

Joint limits and workspace: Servos only rotate so far and links have fixed lengths, so only a region of space is

reachable. Your IK must check reachability and respect limits, or you command the impossible.

▸

Smooth motion: Jumping servos straight to a new angle is jerky. Interpolating between poses over time (in joint space,

or along a straight Cartesian path) makes motion smooth and predictable — the beginning of trajectory planning.

▸

#2

Portable Wind Tunnel with Data Acquisition

FLUIDS • AERODYNAMICS • INSTRUMENTATION

Difficulty: Intermediate | Estimated cost: $40–70

Why recruiters love this: Aerodynamics and fluid mechanics are core ME competencies. Building

your own test equipment shows you understand both the theory and the practical challenges of

measurement — and that you can design experiments, not just run them.

Build a small-scale open-circuit wind tunnel (~30cm test section) with a fan-driven flow, a honeycomb

flow straightener, a contraction nozzle, and an instrumented test section. Use pressure sensors and

an Arduino to measure velocity profiles and drag forces on test objects. Visualize airflow with smoke

or string tufts.

What you need:

• Acrylic or plywood sheets for tunnel walls

• 120mm PC fans (2-3 in series) or a centrifugal blower

• Drinking straws (honeycomb flow straightener — seriously, it works)

• Arduino Mega + BMP280 or differential pressure sensor (MPXV7002DP)

• Small load cell (for drag force measurement)

@1nska  •  6 ME Portfolio Projects  •  Page 7

• Incense sticks for smoke visualization

• 3D-printed airfoil test models (NACA profiles)

Skills it proves:

• Fluid mechanics — boundary layers, pressure distributions, Reynolds number

• Experimental design and data acquisition

• Sensor calibration and uncertainty analysis

• CAD and fabrication of precision test equipment

• Data analysis and visualization (Python + matplotlib)

How to build it:

Step 1: Design the tunnel geometry. Follow established open-circuit wind tunnel design rules:

contraction ratio of 6:1 to 9:1, test section length ~1.5x the width. Sketch it in CAD first to verify

dimensions.

Step 2: Build the structure. Cut acrylic or plywood panels. The test section should be transparent

(acrylic) for visualization. Use silicone sealant on joints to prevent air leaks.

Step 3: Build the flow straightener. Bundle ~200 drinking straws (cut to 10cm) tightly into the

settling chamber. This kills turbulence and creates uniform flow. Add a fine mesh screen after the

straws.

Step 4: Install fans and test airflow. Mount fans at the exit (suction configuration is more uniform

than blowing). Measure velocity at multiple points across the test section to verify uniformity.

Target 5-15 m/s.

Step 5: Set up instrumentation. Wire the differential pressure sensor to a pitot tube for velocity

measurement. Mount the load cell on a sting balance to measure drag. Log all data to the

Arduino at 100+ Hz.

Step 6: Run experiments. 3D-print NACA 0012 and NACA 4412 airfoils. Measure drag at

different angles of attack. Compare your data to published results. Use incense smoke for flow

visualization and photograph it.

Useful links & resources:

• NASA wind tunnel design guide (PDF)

• NACA airfoil coordinate generator

• MPXV7002DP pressure sensor datasheet

• Python matplotlib for data visualization

• Open-source wind tunnel project — MIT

@1nska  •  6 ME Portfolio Projects  •  Page 8

Level up: Add a hot-wire anemometer for turbulence intensity measurements, or use

PIV (Particle Image Velocimetry) with a laser pointer and camera to visualize velocity

fields quantitatively. Publish your results and CAD files as an open-source project.

@1nska  •  6 ME Portfolio Projects  •  Page 9

#3

Dual-Axis Solar Tracker

CONTROL SYSTEMS • RENEWABLE ENERGY • MECHANICAL DESIGN

Difficulty: Intermediate | Estimated cost: $35–55

Why recruiters love this: Renewable energy is booming and every company in the space needs

MEs who understand both the mechanical design and the control systems behind tracking systems.

This project proves you can do both.

Build a dual-axis solar tracker that automatically orients a small solar panel to face the sun throughout

the day. Use light-dependent resistors (LDRs) to detect the sun's position and servo motors to adjust

pan and tilt angles. Log power output data to prove your tracker generates more energy than a fixed

panel.

What you need:

• Small solar panel (5-10W)

• Arduino Uno

• 2x MG996R servo motors (high torque for outdoor use)

• 4x LDR sensors + 10K resistors

• Pan-tilt mounting bracket (3D print or buy)

@1nska  •  6 ME Portfolio Projects  •  Page 10

• INA219 current/voltage sensor for power logging

• Weatherproof enclosure for electronics

Skills it proves:

• Mechanical design for outdoor/environmental conditions

• Control system design — closed-loop sun tracking

• Sensor calibration and signal conditioning

• Energy systems — quantitative performance analysis

• Weatherproofing and design for reliability

How to build it:

Step 1: Design the mount. Create a pan-tilt mechanism with two degrees of freedom. The base

servo controls azimuth (east-west), the top servo controls elevation (up-down). Design for the

weight of your panel + wind loads.

Step 2: Build the LDR sensor array. Mount 4 LDRs in a cross pattern with a divider wall between

them. When the sun is centered, all 4 read equal values. An imbalance tells you which direction

to move.

Step 3: Write the tracking algorithm. Compare opposite LDR pairs: if left > right, rotate left. If top

> bottom, tilt up. Add a dead band (±5%) to prevent hunting/oscillation around the sun position.

Step 4: Add power monitoring. Wire an INA219 sensor to measure the solar panel's voltage and

current output. Log data to an SD card every 30 seconds — you need this data to prove the

tracker works.

Step 5: Set up the comparison test. Place an identical fixed panel next to your tracker. Log both

panels' output simultaneously over a full day. Calculate the energy gain percentage.

Step 6: Analyze and document. Plot power output vs. time for both panels using Python.

Calculate total daily kWh for each. Create graphs showing the tracker's advantage. Document

the full build on GitHub with CAD files and data.

Useful links & resources:

• Solar tracker theory — how tracking increases yield

• INA219 power sensor tutorial — Adafruit

• Pan-tilt bracket 3D print files

• Arduino solar tracker tutorial

• Servo motor selection guide

@1nska  •  6 ME Portfolio Projects  •  Page 11

Level up: Add WiFi logging so you can monitor performance remotely via a web

dashboard. Then add a weather station (temperature, wind speed, cloud cover) and

correlate environmental conditions with tracking performance. This data set becomes

a publishable research project.

#4

PID-Controlled Thermal Management System

HEAT TRANSFER • CONTROL SYSTEMS • EMBEDDED

Difficulty: Intermediate | Estimated cost: $30–50

Why recruiters love this: Thermal management is critical in electronics, automotive, aerospace, and

data centers. Building a PID-controlled cooling system shows you understand heat transfer

fundamentals AND can implement real control loops — the exact combination companies like Tesla,

Apple, and server farm operators need.

Build a smart cooling system that monitors temperature across multiple zones using thermistors, runs

a PID control loop to adjust fan speeds via PWM, and maintains a target temperature within ±0.5°C.

Display real-time data on an LCD and log performance data for analysis.

What you need:

• Arduino Mega

• 3-4x NTC thermistors (10K) for multi-zone sensing

• 2x 12V PWM-controllable fans (Noctua or similar)

• MOSFET modules (IRF520) for fan speed control

• Aluminum heat sink + resistive heater (simulated heat source)

@1nska  •  6 ME Portfolio Projects  •  Page 13

• 16x2 LCD display or OLED (SSD1306)

• 12V power supply + buck converter for Arduino

Skills it proves:

• Heat transfer fundamentals applied in practice

• PID control — tuning, implementation, and performance analysis

• Multi-zone thermal sensing and management

• PWM motor control through MOSFETs

• Data logging and system characterization

How to build it:

Step 1: Build the thermal test bed. Mount a power resistor (10-50W) on an aluminum heat sink as

your heat source. Attach thermistors at different distances from the source to create temperature

zones.

Step 2: Set up fan control. Wire fans through IRF520 MOSFETs connected to Arduino PWM

pins. Verify you can control fan speed from 0-100% smoothly. Measure airflow at different PWM

values.

Step 3: Implement the PID controller. Start with proportional only (P). Set a target temperature

(e.g., 40°C). Gradually add derivative (D) to reduce overshoot, then integral (I) to eliminate

steady-state error.

Step 4: Tune the PID. Use the Ziegler-Nichols method: increase P until oscillation, note the

period, then calculate P, I, D values. Fine-tune from there. Log temperature vs. time to show your

tuning process.

Step 5: Add multi-zone control. Implement independent PID loops for each zone, or a cascaded

controller where the hottest zone drives the primary response. Show the system maintaining all

zones within ±0.5°C.

Step 6: Run step-response tests. Apply sudden heat loads and record how the system responds.

Plot temperature vs. time, fan speed vs. time, and calculate settling time, overshoot, and

steady-state error. This data is your portfolio showpiece.

Useful links & resources:

• PID controller explained — Brian Douglas (YouTube)

• Ziegler-Nichols tuning method

• Arduino PID library

• NTC thermistor guide — Adafruit

• PWM fan control with MOSFET tutorial

@1nska  •  6 ME Portfolio Projects  •  Page 14

Level up: Replace the simple heat source with a real CPU or GPU under load.

Benchmark thermal performance against the stock cooler. If your PID system

maintains lower temps at the same noise level, you've built something companies

would actually ship.

#5

Desktop CNC Engraver (Built From Scratch)

MANUFACTURING • CNC • MECHANICAL DESIGN

Difficulty: Advanced | Estimated cost: $60–100

Why recruiters love this: Understanding CNC from the machine-builder's perspective — not just the

operator's — is rare and incredibly valuable. This project proves you understand linear motion

systems, stepper motor control, G-code, and mechanical precision — the fundamentals of advanced

manufacturing.

Build a small-scale 2-axis (or 3-axis) CNC engraver from scratch that can engrave text and patterns

on wood, acrylic, or aluminum. Use linear rails, stepper motors, and an Arduino with GRBL firmware.

Design the frame, assemble the motion system, and calibrate it to achieve ±0.1mm accuracy.

What you need:

• Arduino Uno + CNC Shield V3

• 2-3x NEMA 17 stepper motors + A4988 drivers

• Linear rails (MGN12) or smooth rods + linear bearings

• GT2 timing belts and pulleys (or lead screws for Z-axis)

• 775 DC spindle motor or Dremel tool

@1nska  •  6 ME Portfolio Projects  •  Page 16

• Aluminum extrusion (2020) or 3D-printed frame

• GRBL firmware (free) + Universal G-code Sender

• 12V 5A+ power supply

Skills it proves:

• Machine design — frame rigidity, motion systems, backlash compensation

• Stepper motor control and CNC kinematics

• G-code programming and CAM workflows

• Precision measurement and calibration

• Manufacturing process understanding from the builder's perspective

How to build it:

Step 1: Design the frame. Use 2020 aluminum extrusion or a rigid 3D-printed structure. Rigidity

is everything — any flex in the frame becomes inaccuracy in your engraving. Model it in CAD and

verify joint stiffness.

Step 2: Build the motion system. Mount linear rails and stepper motors for X and Y axes. Use

GT2 belts for speed or lead screws for precision. Ensure everything is square — measure

diagonals and shim if needed.

Step 3: Wire and flash the controller. Stack the CNC Shield on the Arduino, plug in A4988

drivers, wire stepper motors. Flash GRBL firmware. Use Universal G-code Sender to test jogging

each axis.

Step 4: Calibrate steps/mm. Command a 100mm move, measure the actual travel with calipers.

Adjust the steps/mm in GRBL settings until commanded distance matches actual distance within

±0.1mm.

Step 5: Mount the spindle and test. Attach the spindle motor to the Z-axis (or use a pen for initial

tests). Run a test pattern — a square, a circle, and text. Measure dimensions to verify accuracy.

Step 6: Engrave a real project. Design something in Fusion 360 CAM or Easel, generate G-code,

and engrave it on wood or acrylic. Document the full workflow: CAD → CAM → G-code →

finished part.

#6

Wireless Strain Gauge Bridge Monitor

INSTRUMENTATION • STRUCTURAL • IOT

Difficulty: Advanced | Estimated cost: $45–70

Why recruiters love this: Structural health monitoring is a growing field where ME meets IoT.

Companies in aerospace, civil infrastructure, and automotive need engineers who understand both

the mechanics of deformation AND the electronics of measurement. This project proves you're that

engineer.

Build a wireless strain measurement system using strain gauges in a Wheatstone bridge

configuration, amplified by an instrumentation amplifier, digitized by an HX711 ADC, and transmitted

wirelessly via an ESP32. Apply it to a real structure — a 3D-printed beam under load — and compare

measured strain to FEA predictions.

What you need:

• Foil strain gauges (120Ω, pack of 10)

• HX711 24-bit ADC module (same one used for load cells)

• ESP32 for wireless data transmission

• Instrumentation amplifier (INA125 or AD620) — optional for higher precision

@1nska  •  6 ME Portfolio Projects  •  Page 19

• 3D-printed or aluminum cantilever beam (test specimen)

• Cyanoacrylate adhesive (for bonding strain gauges)

• Known weights for calibration (1-5 kg)

• Cloud platform (ThingSpeak or Firebase)

Skills it proves:

• Strain measurement fundamentals — gauge factor, Wheatstone bridge, signal conditioning

• Analog signal amplification and noise reduction

• Wireless sensor networks and IoT architecture

• FEA validation — comparing simulation to physical measurement

• Data acquisition system design

How to build it:

Step 1: Prepare and bond strain gauges. Surface-prep the test beam (sand, clean, mark

alignment). Apply strain gauges with cyanoacrylate — alignment and adhesion quality directly

affect accuracy. This step requires patience.

Step 2: Build the Wheatstone bridge circuit. Wire gauges in a half-bridge or full-bridge

configuration. Connect to the HX711 ADC. Calibrate the zero point (no load) and verify stability

— readings should be rock steady.

Step 3: Calibrate with known loads. Apply known weights to your cantilever beam. Record

HX711 readings at each load. Create a calibration curve (load vs. digital reading). Calculate

sensitivity and linearity.

Step 4: Set up wireless transmission. Program the ESP32 to read the HX711, apply the

calibration equation, and transmit strain values over WiFi to ThingSpeak or Firebase every

second.

Step 5: Run the FEA comparison. Model your exact beam geometry in Fusion 360 or ANSYS.

Apply the same loads you tested physically. Compare FEA-predicted strain at the gauge location

to your measured values. They should agree within 5-10%.

Step 6: Build the dashboard and document. Create a real-time web dashboard showing live

strain data. Demonstrate the system detecting when load is applied and removed. Document the

FEA vs. measurement comparison — this is gold for interviews.

Useful links & resources:

• Strain gauge bonding guide — HBM

• HX711 Arduino library + tutorial

unexpected strain patterns. This turns a student project into a legitimate structural

health monitoring system.

// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
A two-wheel balancing robot is an inverted pendulum: left alone it falls, so it only stays
upright because a controller is constantly catching it. An IMU measures the tilt, a control
loop computes how to drive the wheels to stay under the centre of mass, and the robot
balances — leaning into a push and recovering. It is the most visually striking build in this
guide and a genuine lesson in controlling an unstable system, sensor fusion, and cascaded
control. If the closed-loop servo taught you to hold a position, this teaches you to
stabilise something that actively wants to fall.

// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

Step 3: Wire the FSR sensors. Mount force-sensitive resistors on the inner surface of each finger

pad. Wire them to the Arduino's analog inputs through a voltage divider circuit (10K resistor).

Step 4: Write the control loop. Read FSR values → compare to target force → adjust servo

position. Start with a simple proportional controller: if force is too high, open slightly; if too low,

close slightly.

Step 5: Test with different objects. Calibrate your force thresholds for soft objects (tomato, egg)

vs hard objects (ball, cube). Record success/failure rates for your documentation.

Step 6: Document everything. Take photos at every stage. Create a GitHub repo with your CAD

files (STL + source), Arduino code, wiring diagram, and a demo video showing the gripper

handling different objects.

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Fire a laser across a gap and clock anything that crosses it — in real units

## why this matters

The simplest thing you can do with light is notice when it stops arriving. Point a laser at a
photodiode and you have a beam; break it and a voltage collapses in microseconds. Put two
beams a known distance apart, time how long an object takes to cross from one to the other,
and you have a speed trap — clock a Nerf dart, a dropped ball, a swinging door. It is the
cheapest possible photonics build, the response is instant and visual, and it teaches the
photodetection front end that every later project in this guide depends on.

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Here's the timeline of my messages:

The follow-up sequence:

• Nov 26: First pitch — the full proposal with venue, concept, and collaboration offer

• Nov 27: Follow-up — "Just checking in to see if there's any update on the robot availability. No rush

at all."

• Dec 1: Second follow-up — "Just wanted to check in again and see if there's any update on which

robot might be available."

Then:

I Them: "Yes, we have it"

I Them: "How long you need"

↑ Three messages. Five days. That's all it took.

Why this works:

• Most people send one message and quit. They interpret silence as rejection. It's usually just

busyness

• Polite persistence is not annoying. Notice my follow-ups always included "no rush" — I was

respectful, not desperate

• Each follow-up had a reason: Checking on availability, finalizing timeline — not just "bumping this"

The rule:

Follow up at least 3 times before assuming it's a no. Space them out (1 day, then 3–4 days). Be

polite. Be specific. And never apologize for following up — it shows you're serious.

I The fortune is in the follow-up. The people who get what they want are simply the ones who don't stop
asking.

@1nska  |  The Robot Framework  |  Page 8

Two days after the final confirmation, an 80–90 kg industrial KUKA robot worth approximately $30,000

arrived at NYU Shanghai.

Their engineers couldn't program it for free — but I could do it myself. They didn't even know I studied

engineering. That was the final piece that made the whole thing click.

I programmed the robot for a live art performance at Fotografiska Shanghai, exploring the theme of

human-robot interaction. A real industrial robot, performing alongside humans, in one of the city's most

visited art spaces.

All because I saved a contact, sent a message, and didn't give up after the first reply.

THE COMPLETE FRAMEWORK
The 5 Steps — Quick Reference

1 — Collect contacts before you need them

Go to every event. Save every contact. You never know which one matters.

2 — Pitch their win, not your need

Frame it as a collaboration. Lead with what they gain. Make them the hero.

3 — Reframe, don’t retreat

When you hit a wall, don't disappear. Reposition the ask. The conversation isn't over until you decide it is.

4 — Make it embarrassingly easy to say yes

Handle everything. Remove friction. Their only job is saying yes.

5 — Follow up like your life depends on it

3 follow-ups minimum. Polite. Persistent. Specific. Don't stop after silence.

@1nska  |  The Robot Framework  |  Page 9

USE THIS FOR
How to Apply This Framework to Anything

This framework isn't just about robots. It works for any situation where you're asking someone "above your

level" for something you think you shouldn't have access to.

Getting an internship

• Step 1: Connect with employees at target companies on LinkedIn months before applying

• Step 2: Don't ask "can you refer me?" — say "I built X that's relevant to your team's work on Y. I'd

love to hear your perspective."

• Step 3: If they say the team isn't hiring, ask "Which teams are? I'm flexible on the role."

• Step 4: Have your portfolio, resume, and project links ready to send instantly

• Step 5: Follow up after 1 week and again after 2 weeks. Attach a new project or insight each time

Finding a mentor

• Step 1: Engage with their content for weeks before reaching out (comments, shares, thoughtful

replies)

• Step 2: Don't ask "will you be my mentor?" — say "I'm working on X and your approach to Y

changed how I think about it. Could I ask you one specific question?"

• Step 3: If they're too busy, ask "Is there someone you'd recommend I talk to?"

• Step 4: Come with a specific question, not a vague "I need guidance." Respect their time

• Step 5: After the conversation, follow up with what you implemented from their advice. This is how

one conversation becomes a relationship

Getting a sponsorship or partnership

• Step 1: Build the relationship before the pitch — attend their events, engage with their brand, know

their goals

• Step 2: Lead with audience numbers, venue prestige, or distribution — what's in it for them?

• Step 3: When they mention budget concerns, offer creative alternatives: logo placement, social

media posts, testimonials

• Step 4: Have a one-pager ready: what you need, what they get, the timeline, and next steps

• Step 5: Follow up with a deadline: "We're finalizing partners by [date] — would love to include you"

@1nska  |  The Robot Framework  |  Page 10

TEMPLATES
Copy-and-Adapt Messages

Here are message templates based on exactly what worked for me. Adapt them to your situation.

The first outreach:

"Hi [Name], we connected at [event/context] a while back. I'm currently working on [project] — [1

sentence about what it is and why it matters]. I think [their company/product] would be a great fit for

[specific collaboration]. Would love to explore this with you if you're open to it."

The budget reframe:

"We don't have a budget for this right now — this is a [non-profit/student/educational] project. That

said, we'd love to position this as a collaboration: [specific benefit to them: visibility,

acknowledgment, content, audience access]. Would this work on your end?"

The follow-up:

"Hi [Name], just checking in to see if there's any update on [specific thing you discussed]. No rush at

all — I just wanted to follow up as we're [reason: finalizing plans / confirming timeline / etc.]. Thanks

so much!"

I Notice: every template is specific, provides value, and respects their time. Never send "just following up"
with no context. Always give them a reason to reply.

@1nska  |  The Robot Framework  |  Page 11

The Bottom Line

The gap between "no" and "yes" is smaller than you think.
Most people never get what they want because they never ask.

Or they ask once, hear silence, and assume it's over.

Don't be most people.

Follow @1nska for build logs, frameworks, and the real story

of building a startup as a student.

Save the contact. Send the message. Follow up.

The robot is closer than you think.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Motors fail, batteries fail, and a drone that loses power becomes a falling brick. A parachute recovery system detects the fall

— or takes a command — kills the motors, and deploys a canopy so the aircraft comes down at a walking pace instead of
terminal velocity. Commercial systems cost hundreds; you can build one with a spring-loaded tube, a servo pin, an

accelerometer, and a properly sized canopy. It is the one upgrade that protects people on the ground as much as the drone, it
is increasingly what regulators want for flights near people, and the deployment shot is spectacular.

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
BUILD NOTE
Don’t write gimbal firmware from scratch. A STorM32 or SimpleBGC-class controller with its IMU handles FOC and

stabilisation; your engineering is the frame, the balance, the motor choice, the tuning, and the vibration mounting.
Balance first — an unbalanced gimbal can never be tuned smooth.
canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Detecting the fall: In freefall the accelerometer reads near zero g on all axes. Detect that condition for longer than a set

time (a few hundred milliseconds, to reject bumps) and you have a reliable trigger. A failsafe signal from the flight

controller, or a manual channel, are the other triggers.

▸

Cut the motors: On deploy, the props must stop instantly, or the canopy and lines wrap into them. The trigger sends a

motor-kill to the flight controller (or cuts ESC power) before the pin releases.

▸

The deployer: A tube holds the packed canopy on a compressed spring, retained by a pin a servo pulls. Release the pin

and the spring throws the canopy clear of the airframe; a bridle and swivel connect it to the frame’s centre.

▸

Sizing the canopy: Descent rate depends on canopy area and total mass; aim for roughly four to five metres per second.
Too small and the landing is a crash; too large and the pack won’t fit. The maths is simple drag physics.
▸

Testing a safety system: Bench trigger tests, then drop tests with a dummy mass from height, then tethered deploy, then
a live test over an empty field. A parachute you haven’t drop-tested is decoration.
▸

[ U P G R A D E 0 3 ]
Parachute Recovery System

A failsafe that senses freefall and pops a canopy — saves the drone, and whoever is

below it

// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

GPS puts a drone down within a couple of metres, which is useless for docking, charging, or landing on a vehicle. Precision

landing uses a downward camera to see a fiducial marker on the pad, computes exactly where the pad is relative to the drone,
and steers the descent so it touches down centred — the technology behind every autonomous docking and charging drone.

Add a small companion computer, a camera, and a printed tag, and your drone lands itself on a pad the size of a coaster. It is
computer vision, coordinate transforms, and controller integration, and the demo is undeniable.

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Fiducials: An AprilTag or ArUco marker is a black-and-white pattern designed for reliable detection; from its corners in the
image, the software recovers the tag’s position and orientation relative to the camera.
▸

The companion computer: A small computer (a Raspberry Pi) runs the camera and the tag detector, then sends the

target’s offset to the flight controller as a standard landing-target message over the telemetry link.

▸

The controller lands on it: In precision-landing mode, the flight controller uses the target offset to steer the descent,

correcting horizontally as it comes down so the drone stays centred over the pad.

▸

Calibration and alignment: Camera calibration turns pixels into angles correctly; camera-to-body alignment turns those

into offsets the controller can act on. Get either wrong and it lands confidently next to the pad.

▸

Losing the target: Tags disappear when the drone is too high, too tilted, or too close. Robust behaviour handles that: keep
the last estimate briefly, then fall back to a normal landing or abort.

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
SP02 · 27.9 °C · ε 0.95

Lift from pressure: Air moving over a curved wing speeds up and its pressure drops relative to the underside; the pressure

difference integrates into lift. Angle the wing up and lift grows — until the flow separates and the wing stalls.

▸

Conditioning the flow: A fan produces swirl and turbulence. A settling chamber slows the air, a honeycomb straightens it,

fine screens break up turbulence, and a contraction (a smooth nozzle) accelerates it into a clean, uniform test-section
flow.

▸

Seeing the flow: A thin stream of smoke (or fog from a small glycol fogger) introduced upstream follows the streamlines,

making the flow over the wing visible — attached flow, the stagnation point, and the separated wake at stall.

▸

Measuring force: Mount the wing on a sting connected to a load cell (or two, for lift and drag). As the fan runs, the load cell

reads the aerodynamic force directly; plot lift against angle of attack to see the lift slope and the stall.

▸

Reynolds number: The key scaling parameter for aerodynamics. Your small, slow tunnel runs at low Reynolds number,

which changes stall behaviour and lift coefficients — so you report airspeed, chord, and Re with every result.

▸

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Every radar on Earth starts with one idea: a moving object shifts the frequency of the radio
it reflects. A pocket microwave module like the HB100 transmits a steady ~10.5 GHz tone and
mixes it with the echo, and what comes out is an audio-frequency “beat” whose pitch is
directly proportional to the target’s speed. Amplify that beat, sample it on an Arduino, run
an FFT, and you can read how fast your hand — or a passing person — is moving, in real time.
It is the cheapest possible way to build genuine radar, the payoff is immediate and visual,
and it is the foundation every later project in this guide builds on.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Motors fail, batteries fail, and a drone that loses power becomes a falling brick. A parachute recovery system detects the fall

— or takes a command — kills the motors, and deploys a canopy so the aircraft comes down at a walking pace instead of
terminal velocity. Commercial systems cost hundreds; you can build one with a spring-loaded tube, a servo pin, an

accelerometer, and a properly sized canopy. It is the one upgrade that protects people on the ground as much as the drone, it
is increasingly what regulators want for flights near people, and the deployment shot is spectacular.
