contr | BUILD NOTE
Don’t write gimbal firmware from scratch. A STorM32 or SimpleBGC-class controller with its IMU handles FOC and

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
BUILD NOTE
Don’t write gimbal firmware from scratch. A STorM32 or SimpleBGC-class controller with its IMU handles FOC and

stabilisation; your engineering is the frame, the balance, the motor choice, the tuning, and the vibration mounting.
Balance first — an unbalanced gimbal can never be tuned smooth.
canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Detecting the fall: In freefall the accelerometer reads near zero g on all axes. Detect that condition for longer than a set

time (a few hundred milliseconds, to reject bumps) and you have a reliable trigger. A failsafe signal from the flight

controller, or a manual channel, are the other triggers.

▸

Cut the motors: On deploy, the props must stop instantly, or the canopy and lines wrap into them. The trigger sends a

motor-kill to the flight controller (or cuts ESC power) before the pin releases.

▸

The deployer: A tube holds the packed canopy on a compressed spring, retained by a pin a servo pulls. Release the pin

and the spring throws the canopy clear of the airframe; a bridle and swivel connect it to the frame’s centre.

▸

Sizing the canopy: Descent rate depends on canopy area and total mass; aim for roughly four to five metres per second.
Too small and the landing is a crash; too large and the pack won’t fit. The maths is simple drag physics.
▸

Testing a safety system: Bench trigger tests, then drop tests with a dummy mass from height, then tethered deploy, then
a live test over an empty field. A parachute you haven’t drop-tested is decoration.
▸

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Most commercial 'night vision' devices cheat — they blast IR LEDs and use a camera. This is visible to

anyone else with night vision and broadcasts your position. Real military night vision (Gen III image

intensifiers) amplifies ambient photons — starlight, moonlight, airglow — without emitting anything.

This project builds a digital equivalent: a high-sensitivity CMOS sensor with a fast lens, gain-adjustable

analog front end, and OLED microdisplay eyepiece. No IR illuminator. No emission. Fully passive.

System Architecture
canonicalDescription.summary:
Passive Night Vision Scope

Image amplification from ambient starlight — zero emission, fully covert | • Fast lens (f/1.0): The lens determines how many photons reach the sensor. An f/1.0 lens collects

4x more light than an f/2.0 lens. CCTV lenses with 25mm focal length and f/1.0-f/1.2 aperture are

available for $5-10. This is the single most import
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• Fast lens (f/1.0): The lens determines how many photons reach the sensor. An f/1.0 lens collects

4x more light than an f/2.0 lens. CCTV lenses with 25mm focal length and f/1.0-f/1.2 aperture are

available for $5-10. This is the single most important component — without a fast lens, no amount

of electronic gain will produce a usable image.

• CMOS sensor (OV7251): A global-shutter monochrome sensor with high NIR sensitivity.

Monochrome sensors are 3-4x more sensitive than color sensors (no Bayer filter absorbing 2/3 of

the photons). The OV7251 has 3µm pixels with good quantum efficiency at 850-950nm — where

@1nska  •  Defense Tech Part 2: Laser + Covert Systems  •  Page 17

night sky airglow provides ambient illumination.

• Gain control (AGC): The sensor's analog gain is adjustable from 1x to 64x. An AGC loop adjusts

the gain based on average image brightness — in darker conditions, gain increases automatically.

Additional digital gain (2-8x) on the processor trades noise for visibility in extreme darkness.

• Image processor (STM32H7 or RPi Zero): Reads the sensor via MIPI CSI or parallel interface.

Applies histogram equalization to maximize contrast. Optionally applies noise reduction (temporal

averaging of 2-4 frames). Outputs to OLED microdisplay.

• OLED microdisplay: A 0.39" or 0.5" OLED microdisplay viewed through an eyepiece lens.

Green phosphor color (matches human scotopic sensitivity) for traditional NV appearance. Refresh

rate: 30fps minimum to avoid flicker.

// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Send audio and data across the room on a beam of light

## why this matters

Fibre-optic internet is just light carrying data down a glass thread — and you can do the
same thing through open air with a laser and a photodiode. Modulate a laser’s brightness with
an audio or digital signal, point it at a photodiode across the room, and recover the signal
on the far side: a free-space optical link, the same idea as Li-Fi and satellite laser comms.
It is a hands-on lesson in modulation, analog front ends, and why light is such a high-
bandwidth carrier — and unlike radio it needs no licence and barely leaks past the beam.

Personal Website

Social Media

• Document your build journey publicly — this is how I grew my audience

@1nska  |  The Dangerously Overeducated Engineer Guide  |  Page 8

BONUS
The Internship Gameplan

If you've followed steps 1–6, you're already ahead of 90% of applicants. Here's how to convert that into

actual offers.

3 months before applications:

• Have at least 2 shipped projects you can demo and explain in detail

• Have your GitHub, LinkedIn, and resume all telling the same story

• Start LeetCode / NeetCode prep — you still need to pass technical screens

• Make a target list of 20–30 companies, prioritized by fit, not prestige

During applications:

• Tailor every resume to the specific role — generic resumes get generic results

• Cold DM engineers at target companies on LinkedIn. Ask genuine questions first

• Apply to startups too — steeper learning curve and they care more about what you've built

• Your projects ARE your pitch. Lead every conversation with what you've shipped

In interviews:

• "Tell me about yourself" = tell them what you've built and why, not your GPA

• For behavioral questions, use your build stories — challenges, tradeoffs, failures

• Think out loud in technical questions. Nobody expects a student to know everything

• Ask smart questions back — about the stack, team, what you'd work on

I Internships don't go to the smartest students. They go to the ones who look like they don't need the
internship to prove they can build. Be that person.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Raw drone footage is a jittery mess because the camera rides every twitch of the airframe. A brushless gimbal fixes that: an

IMU on the camera measures its attitude hundreds of times a second and two brushless motors, driven smoothly with field-
oriented control, hold it level no matter what the drone does. Build one and your footage goes from home video to broadcast-

smooth. It is mechatronics, control, and the same FOC drive technology behind robot joints — and it is the upgrade that most

changes what your drone produces.
canonicalDescription.summary:

controller’s job is to hold that attitude at the target regardless of what the frame beneath it does.
▸

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Sensing the camera’s attitude: An IMU mounted on the camera plate reports its pitch and roll at high rate. The
controller’s job is to hold that attitude at the target regardless of what the frame beneath it does.
▸

Gimbal motors and FOC: Gimbal brushless motors are high-pole-count, low-speed motors driven with field-oriented
control for smooth, cogging-free torque at zero speed — exactly what holding a camera still requires.
▸

The stabilisation loop: A PID loop per axis takes the attitude error and commands motor torque to cancel it. Tuning sets

the stiffness and damping: too soft and it wobbles, too stiff and it oscillates.

▸

Balance is everything: If the camera’s centre of mass sits off the motor axes, the motors fight gravity constantly, wasting

torque and ruining smoothness. Mechanical balance on each axis before any tuning is the golden rule.

▸

Isolating vibration: Motor and prop vibration reaches the gimbal through the frame; rubber dampers between drone and

gimbal filter it so the IMU sees camera motion, not airframe buzz.

▸

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
DO THIS
Not a tutorial — something with a job: a plant-moisture alarm, a desk lamp that dims
with a knob, a door sensor that texts you, a temperature logger for your room. Pick
one, make a parts list, build it on a breadboard, then solder it onto perfboard and

put it in a box.

THE TRAP
Ten half-finished projects. One finished thing you use every day teaches more than

ten demos, and it's the one you'll show people.

YOU'RE DONE WHEN
It's been running on your desk for a week and you've fixed at least one thing that

broke.

the build list · @1nska
4

## the $60 starter bench

• Arduino Uno clone starter kit (board, breadboard, wires, LEDs, resistors, buttons,

buzzer, pot, sensors) — $30–40
• Digital multimeter with continuity beep — $15

• Temperature-controlled soldering iron kit + solder + flux — $20–25

• Through-hole soldering practice kit — $5
• USB cable and a phone charger as your 5 V supply — $0

• Later, not now: ESP32 board ($6) once you want Wi-Fi, a basic oscilloscope ($60+)
once you care about signals

## the first five builds, in order

• Blink — change the timing, then blink two LEDs alternately
• Button-controlled LED — learn INPUT_PULLUP and why the button reads backwards

• Buzzer melody — tone() and a short array of notes
• Potentiometer dimmer — analogRead in, PWM out with analogWrite

• Light-sensor night light — a photoresistor in a voltage divider turns the LED on in
the dark

## the only theory you need for month one

• Ohm's law, V = IR: picks every resistor you'll ever add.

• Kirchhoff's current and voltage laws: what goes in comes out; voltages around a
loop add to zero. That's how you reason about any circuit.
• Series vs parallel: series shares current, parallel shares voltage.

• Voltage divider: two resistors turn any sensor into a readable voltage.
• LED current limiting: (5 V - 2 V) / 220 ohm is about 14 mA — bright and safe.

• Pull-up and pull-down resistors: why a floating input reads random noise.

• PWM: switching fast enough that a dimmer looks smooth to your eye.

the build list · @1nska
5

## why this order

→ Why build before reading?

theory read without a circuit in front of you evaporates in a week; theory read to

explain something you just watched happen sticks for years. The kit costs less than
the textbook.

→ Why an Arduino instead of a bare microcontroller?

the Uno hides nothing that matters to a beginner — you still wire every resistor

and read every pin — but it removes the toolchain and programmer setup that stops

most people before the first blink. Move to bare chips or an ESP32 when a project
needs it.

→ Why a multimeter before an oscilloscope?

a meter tells you what's true right now, and almost every beginner bug is a wrong

voltage or an open wire. A scope shows how a signal changes over time, which you
won't need until you're debugging PWM, serial or audio.

That's the whole roadmap.

Six steps, one kit, one project you keep. Everything past this — motors, radios, PCBs,

power supplies — is the same loop: build the small version, then read exactly the theory
you just used, then measure it.

Comment LEARN on the reel and I'll send you this guide. Follow for the next one
— the first five builds, step by step.

— Enes (@1nska) · Electrical Engineering student

// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Sweep a laser line across an object and rebuild it in 3D

## why this matters

A camera sees a flat image; add a laser and geometry and you can recover depth. Project a
thin laser line onto an object, watch from a camera offset to one side, and the line bends
along the object’s contours — measure that bend and triangulation gives you the surface’s 3D
shape. Sweep the line across the object and you reconstruct a full 3D model, the same
structured-light principle behind many 3D scanners and depth cameras. It is the most
ambitious optical build here and a direct lesson in the camera-plus-light geometry at the
core of 3D vision.

// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

canonicalDescription.purpose:
AI can now generate photorealistic images of anyone, anywhere. There is no software-only way to

prove a photo is real. But hardware can. This badge uses a secure cryptographic element (ATECC608)

to sign a hash of: live camera image + GPS coordinates + timestamp. The private key never leaves the

chip — it physically cannot be extracted. The resulting QR code is cryptographic proof that a real

person was physically at a specific location at a specific time.

System Architecture
canonicalDescription.summary:
Deepfake-Proof Identity Badge

Wearable PCB with crypto element that signs live photo + timestamp + GPS | • Camera module: OV2640 or ArduCAM Mini captures a 640x480 JPEG image. Connected to

ESP32 via SPI.

• GPS module: NEO-6M provides latitude, longitude, and UTC timestamp. Connected via UART.

• ATECC608B: Microchip's secure element. Stores an ECC P-2
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• Camera module: OV2640 or ArduCAM Mini captures a 640x480 JPEG image. Connected to

ESP32 via SPI.

• GPS module: NEO-6M provides latitude, longitude, and UTC timestamp. Connected via UART.

• ATECC608B: Microchip's secure element. Stores an ECC P-256 private key in tamper-resistant

hardware. The key is generated on-chip and NEVER leaves. Signs a SHA-256 hash via I2C

command. This is the same chip used in AWS IoT authentication.

@1nska  •  6 AI-Era EE Projects  •  Page 12

• ESP32: Captures photo, reads GPS, computes SHA-256 hash of (image + lat/long + timestamp),

sends hash to ATECC608 for signing, generates a QR code containing the signature + public key

+ metadata.

• E-Paper display: Shows the QR code. Anyone can scan it and verify the signature against the

public key. If the image, location, or time has been tampered with, verification fails.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
The future of AI hardware is moving away from digital clocked computation toward analog, event-driven

processing. Neuromorphic computing mimics biological neurons: instead of sampling signals at a fixed

clock rate, circuits fire 'spikes' only when input changes. This is massively more power-efficient and is

the basis for chips like Intel's Loihi and IBM's TrueNorth. This project builds the fundamental building

block: an analog integrate-and-fire neuron that fuses multiple sensor inputs.

System Architecture
canonicalDescription.summary:
Neuromorphic Sensor Fuser

Analog circuits that process sensor data the way neurons do — no clock, no ADC | • Sensor inputs: Three analog sensors (temperature, pressure, IMU) produce continuous voltage

signals. No ADC — the analog voltages feed directly into the neuron circuits.

• Integrate-and-fire neuron: An RC circuit integrates the input current. Whe
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• Sensor inputs: Three analog sensors (temperature, pressure, IMU) produce continuous voltage

signals. No ADC — the analog voltages feed directly into the neuron circuits.

• Integrate-and-fire neuron: An RC circuit integrates the input current. When the capacitor

voltage reaches a threshold (set by a comparator), the circuit 'fires' — producing a short pulse —

and the capacitor resets via a discharge MOSFET. Higher input = faster firing rate. This is exactly

how biological neurons encode signal strength as spike frequency.

@1nska  •  6 AI-Era EE Projects  •  Page 15

• Synaptic weights: Resistors between sensor outputs and neuron inputs act as analog weights.

A 10K resistor = weak connection. A 1K resistor = strong connection. Changing resistor values

changes how much each sensor influences the output — this is the analog equivalent of neural

network weights.

• Output layer: A second integrate-and-fire neuron receives weighted spikes from the first layer.

Its firing rate represents the fused decision. Connect to an LED or frequency counter to visualize

the output spike train.

Build an application that lets users upload their own documents (PDFs, notes, articles) and have a

conversation with them. The system chunks documents, creates embeddings, stores them in a vector

context.

Distributed Task Queue System

throughput, queue depth, and failure rates. Include retry with exponential backoff, dead letter queues,

success/failure rate, and average processing time. Use Grafana or build a simple React

Difficulty: Advanced | Estimated time: 3-5 weekends

Why recruiters love this: This is the project that makes engineers say "wait, you built that as a

student?" Writing an interpreter proves deep CS fundamentals — parsing, tree traversal, scope

management, type systems. Very few students attempt this, which makes it an instant differentiator.

Build a tree-walking interpreter for a simple programming language you design. It should support

variables, arithmetic, conditionals, loops, functions with parameters, and print output. Write it in

Python, JavaScript, or Go. Include a REPL (interactive console) and the ability to run script files.

Tech stack:

@1nska  •  6 CS Portfolio Projects  •  Page 18

• Lexical analysis — tokenization, regular expressions

• Parsing — recursive descent, Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs)

How to build it:

Step 1: Build the lexer (tokenizer). Read source code character by character. Output a stream of

tokens: NUMBER, STRING, IDENTIFIER, PLUS, MINUS, LET, IF, FUNCTION, etc. Handle edge

cases like multi-character operators (==, !=) and string escaping.

Step 2: Build the parser. Take the token stream and produce an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST).

Use recursive descent parsing. Start with expressions (math), then add statements (let, print),

then control flow (if/else, while), then functions.

Step 3: Build the evaluator. Walk the AST and execute each node. Implement an Environment

class for variable scoping. Handle nested scopes (functions should have their own scope that can

access parent scope).

Step 4: Add functions. This is where it gets interesting. Functions need parameter binding, local

scope, return values, and (optionally) closures. Test with recursive functions like fibonacci and

factorial.

Step 5: Add error handling with line numbers. When something goes wrong (undefined variable,

type mismatch), show the exact line number and a helpful error message. Good errors separate

a toy from a real tool.

Step 6: Build the REPL and file runner. Create an interactive mode where users type

expressions and see results immediately. Also support running .mylang script files. Publish on

GitHub with example programs and a playground.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Every GPS satellite carries an atomic clock, and the timing signal it broadcasts is disciplined to within
nanoseconds of the global time standard. A GPS-disciplined oscillator borrows that accuracy: it takes
the once-per-second pulse (1PPS) from a cheap GPS receiver and uses it to steer a local crystal
oscillator so its frequency is locked, long-term, to atomic precision — parts-per-billion or better. This is
the quiet workhorse of every serious RF lab, cellular base station, and test bench: the reference that
everything else is measured against. Building one teaches you precision timing, control loops, and the
discipline of measuring frequency accurately — and it is the most affordable project in this guide.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand precision frequency references, phase-locked
control loops, GNSS timing (1PPS), oscillator steering via DAC or varactor, and how to characterize
stability with Allan deviation. Timing and synchronization is foundational to communications, radar,
and instrumentation — and surprisingly few engineers actually understand it.

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• The 1PPS reference: A GPS receiver outputs a one-pulse-per-second signal whose rising edge is
aligned to GPS system time — itself steered by the atomic clocks aboard the satellites. The edge is
accurate to tens of nanoseconds, but it jitters pulse-to-pulse, so it is a great long-term reference and
a poor short-term one.

• The local oscillator: An OCXO (oven-controlled crystal oscillator) is extremely stable
second-to-second but slowly drifts over hours and temperature. It is the opposite of GPS: great
short-term, poor long-term. The whole idea is to combine the two.

• Phase comparison: The MCU divides the OCXO (e.g. 10 MHz) down to 1 Hz and measures the time
error between that and the GPS 1PPS using a hardware timer's input capture. This error, in
nanoseconds, is the signal the control loop drives to zero.

• The loop filter: A slow software control loop — a long time constant of many seconds to minutes —
averages out the GPS jitter and computes a correction. Too fast and you chase GPS noise; too
slow and you fail to track drift. This tradeoff is the heart of the design.

• Steering the oscillator: The correction drives a DAC that sets the OCXO's electronic frequency
control (EFC) voltage, nudging it a few parts-per-billion. Over minutes the loop converges and the
OCXO is disciplined — its frequency now traceable to the same standard as the satellites overhead.

@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Reach Space   •   Page 17

protective structures get designed.

propeller can be heard kilometres away. That efficiency is why sonar, not radar, sees underwater.

▸

The hydrophone: A piezoelectric element turns pressure waves into voltage. Potting it in epoxy (or oil-filling a rubber
housing) waterproofs it while coupling sound in; a low-noise preamp right at the element lifts the tiny signal before the

cable adds noise.

▸

Listening: Feed the preamp into an audio interface and you hear the underwater world — engines, rain, fish, wakes. A

spectrogram shows the tonals of a propeller (its blade-rate lines) that identify a vessel.

▸

Bearing from two ears: Two hydrophones a known distance apart receive the same sound at slightly different times. That
time difference of arrival, measured by cross-correlating the two channels, gives the angle the sound came from — the

same trick your ears use.

▸

Ambiguity and range: Two hydrophones give a bearing with a left / right ambiguity; three resolve it; moving or multiple

stations can triangulate range. Real towed arrays are just many hydrophones doing this at scale.

        magnitude = np.abs(samples)

        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:

    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
GPS-denied indoor positioning

place three UWB anchors around a room and trilaterate a tag on the drone to ±10 cm — how
warehouse drones fly where GPS can't reach.

## why this matters

Indoor drones are the fastest-growing part of the industry — warehouse inventory, tunnel and
tank inspection — and none of them have GPS. This project is the answer those teams actually
use: ultra-wideband ranging. Three ESP32 + DW1000 anchors on tripods, one tag on the airframe,
two-way ranging that times a radio pulse round trip to nanoseconds, and trilateration that
turns three distances into an x/y position on a laptop map. You will learn why UWB can range
to centimetres when WiFi cannot, why antenna delay calibration is the whole game, and why
three anchors give you a position but four give you a sanity check. The logged position trace
as you walk a square is proof you can build a localization system, not just call a library.

real, not some dorm room project"

partnership, not a handout

I'm helping them, not the other way around

The rule:

Never ask "can you help me?" Ask "here's how we can work together." Make them the hero of the

story, not the donor.

// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Every processor emits electromagnetic radiation proportional to its switching activity. Different

instructions draw different currents, creating unique EM signatures. Published research (Batina et al.)

has demonstrated that you can extract neural network architectures from EM emissions alone. This

project builds the capture tool: a near-field probe, low-noise amplifier, and SDR-based analysis

pipeline.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand RF signal chain design, low-noise

analog, EM compatibility, and DSP. This is the intersection of analog, RF, and

security — exactly where the highest-paying EE jobs live.

System Architecture

Captures magnetic field emissions within a few cm of the target IC. The small aperture gives

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
@1nska  •  6 AI-Era EE Projects  •  Page 6

• Near-field H-probe: A small loop antenna (10-20mm diameter) made from semi-rigid coax.

Captures magnetic field emissions within a few cm of the target IC. The small aperture gives

spatial selectivity — you can probe individual chips.

• Low-noise amplifier (LNA): A 30dB gain LNA (SPF5189Z or MAR-6+) with 50Ω input

impedance. NF < 1dB. Powered via bias tee from the SDR or external 5V. Critical: proper input

matching and bypass caps or you amplify noise, not signal.

• Bandpass filter: 10-500MHz range covers most digital switching activity. A simple LC filter or a

commercial SAW filter removes out-of-band interference (WiFi, cellular, broadcast FM).

• RTL-SDR: The RTL2832U-based SDR dongle samples the filtered signal. 8-bit ADC, up to 2.4

MSPS bandwidth. Connect via USB to a laptop running Python.

• Analysis (Python): Use pyrtlsdr to capture IQ samples. Run spectrogram (short-time FFT) and

correlate spectral patterns with known instruction sequences. Different AES rounds, different ML

inference stages, idle vs. active — all have distinct signatures.

        magnitude = np.abs(samples)

        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()

I Them: "Is there any budget for renting?"

↑ This is the moment 99% of people disappear. They see this and think "it's over."

I had zero budget. Literally nothing. But instead of saying "never mind" or going silent, I reframed the

entire ask:

I You: "At the moment we don't have a budget allocated for renting. Since this is a non-profit student art
performance, we were hoping you might support it as an educational collaboration."

↑ "Educational collaboration" — two words that turned a rejection into a conversation.

Why this works:

• I didn’t lie or dodge: I was honest about having no budget. Transparency builds trust

• I reframed immediately: Instead of "I can’t pay," I offered "educational collaboration" — a category

companies already have processes for

• I kept the door open: "We were hoping" is soft, respectful, and invites them to find a way — not

demands one

The rule:

When someone asks a question that feels like a dead end, don't retreat. Reframe. "I can't afford it"

becomes "here's what I can offer instead." The conversation isn't over until you decide it is.

// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• Choosing the transmitter: Dedicated beacons like the French GRAVES radar (143.05 MHz) are
ideal where receivable; elsewhere, distant analog TV or FM carriers, or amateur beacons, serve the
same role. You tune precisely to the carrier and look for reflections, not the direct signal.

• Detecting the ping: Software (SDR# plus a spectrogram, or a dedicated detector) shows a waterfall
of the narrow frequency around the carrier. A meteor appears as a sudden bright trace — often
Doppler-shifted as the trail drifts — lasting from a fraction of a second to many seconds for a bright
fireball.

• Counting and timing: Logging pings over hours reveals meteor activity, including the dramatic rise
during showers like the Perseids. Because radio does not care about daylight or clouds, you detect
meteors a visual observer never could — including the daytime showers.

Guessing. 'It doesn't work' is not a diagnosis. 'Pin 13 is at 4.9 V but the LED anode

STEP 06
Build one real project you actually want to use.

DO THIS
Not a tutorial — something with a job: a plant-moisture alarm, a desk lamp that dims
with a knob, a door sensor that texts you, a temperature logger for your room. Pick
one, make a parts list, build it on a breadboard, then solder it onto perfboard and

put it in a box.

THE TRAP
Ten half-finished projects. One finished thing you use every day teaches more than

ten demos, and it's the one you'll show people.

YOU'RE DONE WHEN
It's been running on your desk for a week and you've fixed at least one thing that

broke.

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
L298N enable pin. Verify the motor speed changes smoothly with the knob. Display RPM on the

OLED. This is your baseline — open loop, no feedback.

Step 3: Write the PID algorithm from scratch. Error = setpoint - actualRPM. P_term = Kp × error.

I_term += Ki × error × dt. D_term = Kd × (error - lastError) / dt. Output = P + I + D. Constrain to

0-255. Don't use a PID library — write it yourself so you can explain every line.

Step 4: Tune using Ziegler-Nichols. Set Ki=0, Kd=0. Increase Kp until the system oscillates

steadily — note this as Ku and the oscillation period as Tu. Set Kp=0.6×Ku, Ki=2×Kp/Tu,

Kd=Kp×Tu/8. Fine-tune from there.

Step 5: Add Serial Plotter output. Print setpoint and actual RPM at 50Hz. Open Arduino Serial

Plotter — you'll see both lines. Change the setpoint suddenly and watch the step response.

Screenshot this — it shows overshoot, settling time, and steady-state error.

Step 6: Document everything. Your GitHub README should include: the PID block diagram, your

tuning process, step response screenshots showing before/after tuning, and a table of your final

Kp/Ki/Kd values. This is the data that proves you understand controls.

// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Outdoors, GPS tells the flight controller where the drone is. Indoors there is no GPS, and a drone drifts like a balloon in a draft.

The fix is the same trick an optical mouse uses: a tiny downward camera (a PMW3901 optical-flow sensor) watches the floor
texture slide by and reports velocity, while a rangefinder gives height. Feed both to the flight controller and it holds position —

a hover you can let go of, indoors, that stays put. It is the cheapest, most dramatic upgrade there is, and it is the foundation

for every kind of indoor autonomy.
canonicalDescription.summary:
Optical flow: The sensor sees floor texture move across its tiny image and reports pixel displacement per frame — the

angular rate of the ground beneath. It is a mouse sensor pointed at the floor from a metre up.

▸

Height turns flow into velocity:
canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Optical flow: The sensor sees floor texture move across its tiny image and reports pixel displacement per frame — the

angular rate of the ground beneath. It is a mouse sensor pointed at the floor from a metre up.

▸

Height turns flow into velocity: The same angular rate means a faster ground speed when you are higher, so the flight

controller needs the height from a rangefinder (a ToF like the VL53L1X or a TFmini) to scale flow into linear velocity.

▸

Fusion in the estimator: The flight controller’s EKF fuses flow velocity with the IMU and the rangefinder into a position
estimate whose drift is bounded by the flow — no GPS required. It also enables terrain-following altitude hold.
▸

Light and texture: Flow needs texture and light: a blank floor or a dim room starves it. A small downward LED and a
textured surface make the difference between a locked hover and a drift.
▸

Flight modes: With flow enabled, position-hold and loiter modes work indoors, and the controller arbitrates between GPS

and flow depending on what is healthy. Understanding that arbitration is what keeps a hybrid indoor / outdoor flight safe.

▸

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Vision and touch are biologically synchronized — you see an object and your brain predicts what it will

feel like before you touch it. This glove makes that prediction explicit. A small camera identifies the

material and texture of the object you're reaching for; an AI model maps that material to a haptic

vibration pattern; the pattern plays on motors in the fingertips and palm. You 'feel' surfaces from 10cm

away. Applications: enhanced accessibility for the visually impaired, VR/AR interaction, training for

delicate manipulation tasks (surgery, archaeology, jewelry).

System Architecture
canonicalDescription.summary:
Tactile Sense Augmentation Glove

Feel objects from a distance. AI predicts touch before contact. | • Camera on the back of the hand: A small camera (OV5640 or similar) points outward from the

back of the hand, capturing whatever the hand is reaching for. Streaming at 15fps to the on-glove

processor.

• IMU for hand pose: A 9-DOF IMU provides han
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• Camera on the back of the hand: A small camera (OV5640 or similar) points outward from the

back of the hand, capturing whatever the hand is reaching for. Streaming at 15fps to the on-glove

processor.

• IMU for hand pose: A 9-DOF IMU provides hand orientation and movement direction. This

contextualizes the camera image — knowing the hand is reaching forward changes what counts as

'about to be touched.'

@1nska  •  6 Physical AI Embodiment Projects  •  Page 18

• Material classifier: An edge ML model (MobileNet-Tiny or similar) trained to classify materials

from images: wood, metal, fabric, plastic, glass, paper, skin. Quantized and deployed on a

Raspberry Pi Zero 2W or similar edge compute platform mounted on the wrist.

• Distance + texture estimator: A second model estimates distance to the object (using parallax

from hand motion + IMU data) and surface texture (smooth, rough, grainy) from image features.

• Haptic pattern generator: Maps material+texture+distance to a vibration pattern. Wood = slow

steady pulse on the index fingertip. Metal = sharp, high-frequency pulse on the thumb. Smooth

surfaces = single steady vibration; rough surfaces = irregular pattern. Distance modulates intensity

— stronger as you approach.

• 16-channel PWM motor array: 16 ERM coin motors distributed on the fingertips (3 per finger)

and palm. Each motor driven by an independent PWM channel on a PCA9685 expander. The

pattern generator updates all 16 PWM values 100x per second.

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
After he showed interest, he started asking practical questions: What demo? How big? What date? This is

where most pitches fall apart — people have the vision but can't answer the logistics.

Every time he had a constraint, I adapted:

I Them: "How big is the robot you want"

I You: "Any size is completely fine — the 40cm was just an example. We can adapt the performance concept
to whatever robot you have available."

↑ I didn't push for a specific robot. I wrapped my concept around their constraints.

When he said they didn't have a small robot, I didn't panic. I said we'd adapt. When he asked about the

demo concept, I had the theme ready (human-robot interaction) but kept it flexible enough to fit whatever

they offered.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
When a CubeSat is ejected from its deployer it is tumbling, and before it can do anything useful it has
to stop spinning and stabilize — a maneuver called detumbling. The clever part: it has nothing to push
against, so it pushes against Earth itself. Electromagnets called magnetorquers create a magnetic
moment that interacts with Earth's magnetic field to produce a tiny torque, bleeding off the spin. This
project builds exactly that: coils on a platform, a magnetometer to sense rotation, and the famous
'B-dot' control law that drives the coils to kill the tumble. It is one of the most elegant ideas in spacecraft
engineering — steering against a planet's magnetic field — and it is genuinely buildable and cheap.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand magnetic actuation, the B-dot detumbling control
law, magnetometer sensing and the geomagnetic field, and coil/driver design. Magnetorquers are
flown on most CubeSats, and demonstrating detumbling control is a direct, recognizable ADCS skill.

→ The job this maps to: spacecraft attitude control (ADCS) — CubeSat and smallsat companies, and
ADCS subsystem teams.

@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Build a Real Satellite   •   Page 10
canonicalDescription.summary:
Coils that push against Earth's magnetic field to stop a tumbling platform — how a
CubeSat stabilizes after launch | • Pushing against a planet: A magnetorquer is just a coil; running current through it creates a
magnetic dipole. That dipole tries to align with Earth's magnetic field — like a compass needle —
producing a torque on the spacecraft. With no reaction m
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• Pushing against a planet: A magnetorquer is just a coil; running current through it creates a
magnetic dipole. That dipole tries to align with Earth's magnetic field — like a compass needle —
producing a torque on the spacecraft. With no reaction mass needed, it is an almost-free way to
control attitude in low orbit.

• Sensing the tumble: A 3-axis magnetometer measures Earth's field in the spacecraft's frame. If the
spacecraft is rotating, that measured field vector sweeps around — and the rate at which it changes
(its derivative) tells you how fast you are tumbling. This is the key insight behind the control law.

• The B-dot control law: B-dot drives each coil proportional to the rate of change of the measured field
(the 'B-dot' signal), in the direction that opposes the change. The result is a torque that always fights
the tumble, smoothly bleeding off rotational energy until the field stops sweeping. It needs no
knowledge of absolute orientation, which is why it is so robust.

• Driving the coils: An H-bridge per axis lets the controller push current either direction through each
coil, so it can torque whichever way is needed. Coil current sets the dipole strength; the bigger the
coil and current, the more torque — traded against power and heat.

• Demonstrating it on the ground: Hang the platform on a thin thread (a torsion pendulum) or float it
on a bearing, give it a spin, and watch the B-dot controller drive the coils to slow and stop it relative
to Earth's field. The same algorithm runs on real CubeSats minutes after deployment.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
GOES (Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites) are the spacecraft behind every weather
forecast you have ever seen. They sit in geostationary orbit 35,786 km above the equator, locked to
one spot on Earth, and continuously broadcast imagery back down on an L-band downlink near 1.69
GHz. The operational satellites — GOES-19 (East) and GOES-18 (West) — transmit a signal called
HRIT that anyone can receive with a software-defined radio, a low-noise amplifier, and a dish you can
build from hardware-store parts. Because the satellite never moves relative to the ground, you aim your
antenna once and leave it — no tracking motor. The challenge is pure RF: the signal arrives near the
thermal noise floor after a 36,000 km trip, so the whole link budget hinges on a clean, low-noise front
end and enough antenna gain to close the link.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand L-band RF, low-noise amplifier and noise-figure
design, link budgets, antenna gain, and digital demodulation of a BPSK downlink. These are the
exact skills behind satellite communications, GPS, radar, and every space-to-ground link in the
industry.

@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Reach Space   •   Page 3
canonicalDescription.summary:
Pull a live, full-disk image of the entire planet off a satellite parked 36,000 km up | • Geostationary downlink (1.69 GHz): GOES-East (GOES-19) and GOES-West (GOES-18)
broadcast HRIT near 1694.1 MHz. The signal is BPSK at roughly 400 kSym/s and carries full-disk
Earth images, regional mesoscale scans, and weather products.

• Antenna —
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• Geostationary downlink (1.69 GHz): GOES-East (GOES-19) and GOES-West (GOES-18)
broadcast HRIT near 1694.1 MHz. The signal is BPSK at roughly 400 kSym/s and carries full-disk
Earth images, regional mesoscale scans, and weather products.

• Antenna — gain is everything: After a 36,000 km path the signal is extremely weak, so you need
directional gain. A repurposed 2.4 GHz WiFi grid dish, a small offset satellite dish with a helical
feed, or a DIY cookware reflector all work. Because the bird is geostationary, you point once and
bolt it down.

• Low-noise amplifier + SAW filter: An LNA with a sub-1 dB noise figure, mounted right at the
antenna feed, sets the system sensitivity. A SAW filter near 1.69 GHz rejects cellular and WiFi that
would otherwise desensitize the receiver. This LNA-at-the-antenna placement is the single most
important decision in the build.

• Bias tee + SDR: A bias tee injects DC up the coax to power the LNA at the mast while passing RF
down to the radio. An RTL-SDR (or Airspy for more headroom) digitizes the filtered signal and
streams IQ samples to a laptop or Raspberry Pi.

• Demodulation + decode (SatDump): SatDump locks the BPSK carrier, recovers symbol timing,
applies Viterbi and Reed-Solomon forward error correction, and reassembles the packets into
full-disk and mesoscale images — the same pictures meteorologists use, pulled out of the air by
you.

// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

canonicalDescription.purpose:
A gripper that only knows its finger position will crush a strawberry and drop a coffee cup. Give it a sense of touch — a force

sensor in the fingertip and a control loop on grip force — and it can pick up an egg, a paper cup, or a tool with just the right

squeeze. Building one teaches force sensing, compliant mechanisms, and force control as opposed to position control,
which is the difference between industrial pick-and-place and robots that can handle the messy, fragile real world. It is a

compact, satisfying build with an unforgettable demo.
canonicalDescription.summary:
A gripper that feels how hard it's squeezing — grab an egg without breaking it | BUILD NOTE

Use the tooling: a Raspberry Pi running ROS 2 with a cheap 2D LiDAR (RPLidar A1 or LD19) and the slam_toolbox

and Nav2 packages gets you a working map and navigation without writing SLAM from scratch. Learn what the

packages do first; g
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
BUILD NOTE

Use the tooling: a Raspberry Pi running ROS 2 with a cheap 2D LiDAR (RPLidar A1 or LD19) and the slam_toolbox

and Nav2 packages gets you a working map and navigation without writing SLAM from scratch. Learn what the

packages do first; go deeper on the algorithms once it drives.

Odometry, and why it drifts: Counting wheel rotations gives you a position estimate, but wheel slip and small errors

accumulate, so odometry alone wanders off within metres. It is a good short-term guess and a bad long-term truth.

▸

LiDAR scans the room: A spinning 2D LiDAR returns hundreds of range measurements per revolution — a slice of the

surrounding walls. Each scan is a snapshot of what the world looks like from where the robot is.

▸

SLAM: scan matching: SLAM compares each new scan to the map so far, finds the pose that best aligns them, corrects

the odometry drift, and adds the scan to the map. Localisation and mapping improve each other — the “simultaneous” in

SLAM.

▸

The occupancy grid: The map is a grid where each cell is free, occupied, or unknown, built up from the scans. That grid

is what the planner reasons over.

▸

Planning and navigation: Given the map and a goal, a planner (A* over a costmap that inflates obstacles) finds a path,

and a local controller drives it while dodging anything new. The robot is now autonomous in a space it built its own

model of.

▸

behind military tactical radios (and, historically, a patent from Hedy Lamarr). It is a superb

lesson in resilient communications: synchronisation, spread spectrum, and applied cryptography, all

on cheap radio modules.

import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()

        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

canonicalDescription.purpose:
A large steel object — a vehicle, a pipe, a ship — distorts the Earth’s magnetic field around it,

and a sensitive magnetometer can detect that distortion from a distance, with no contact and no

emission. This is magnetic anomaly detection (MAD), used in defense for submarine hunting and mine

detection, and in the civilian world for archaeology, geophysics, and utility locating. Building one

teaches you to pull a tiny anomaly out of a large, noisy background field — a purely passive sensing

skill with the same signal-in-noise flavour as the RF work, but in the magnetic domain.
canonicalDescription.summary:
Sense a hidden vehicle by the dent it makes in Earth's magnetic field | The geophone: A geophone is a coil-and-magnet transducer that outputs a voltage proportional to

ground velocity. Footsteps and vehicles couple energy into the ground as low-frequency waves the

geophone picks up.

▸

The frequency band: Seismic even
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
The geophone: A geophone is a coil-and-magnet transducer that outputs a voltage proportional to

ground velocity. Footsteps and vehicles couple energy into the ground as low-frequency waves the

geophone picks up.

▸

The frequency band: Seismic events of interest live at low frequencies — footsteps a few to tens

of Hz, vehicles lower and more continuous. Amplify and band-pass this range while rejecting wind,

mains hum, and higher-frequency noise.

▸

Detecting an event: A footstep is a short impulsive burst; the detector watches signal energy

rise above the background floor and flags an event, much like triggering on a noise-adaptive

threshold.

▸

Classifying the source: A person produces distinct, spaced impulses at a walking cadence; a

vehicle produces continuous, lower-frequency energy. Looking at frequency content and rhythm lets

you tell them apart — simple classification from a single sensor.

▸

Siting and range: Coupling to firm ground, sensor depth, and soil type dominate range and

sensitivity. Where and how you plant the sensor matters as much as the electronics — the

practical heart of unattended sensing.

▸

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Every ship, aircraft, drone, and vehicle depends on GNSS for position and precise time, which makes

it one of the most important — and most contested — signals in defense. Building a receiver is the

way in: a $12 module locks onto satellites 20,000 km overhead and hands you latitude, longitude,

altitude, and nanosecond-grade time, and with an SDR you can even glimpse the raw signal buried

below the noise floor. Understanding how GNSS works, and why it is so fragile, is foundational to

positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) engineering — one of the largest and most strategically

vital areas of defense EE.
canonicalDescription.summary:
Pull position and time out of signals from 20,000 km up — and learn how

they're attacked | Trilateration from time: Each satellite broadcasts its position and an extremely precise time.

The receiver measures how long each signal took to arrive, converts that to a distance, and

solves for its own position where the ranges intersect — need
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
Trilateration from time: Each satellite broadcasts its position and an extremely precise time.

The receiver measures how long each signal took to arrive, converts that to a distance, and

solves for its own position where the ranges intersect — needing at least four satellites to also

solve for its own clock error.

▸

Time is the real product: Because position comes from timing, GNSS is first a time system. The

satellites carry atomic clocks and the receiver recovers time to nanoseconds — which is why GNSS

quietly synchronises power grids, cell networks, and financial systems, and why time itself is a

defense priority.

▸

Below the noise floor: The signal arriving at your antenna is weaker than the background noise.

The receiver recovers it by correlating against each satellite’s known pseudo-random code — a

huge processing gain that pulls the signal up out of the noise.

▸

Reading the output: A receiver module outputs standard NMEA sentences over serial: position,

altitude, speed, satellites in view, and fix quality. Parsing these is your window into what the

receiver is actually doing.

▸

Why it is fragile: The received power is tiny, so a small interferer can jam it, and because the

format is public, a fake stronger signal can spoof it. Real systems defend with directional and

adaptive antennas, multi-constellation receivers, and spoofing detection — the resilience side of

PNT.

▸

Step 4: Tune using Ziegler-Nichols. Set Ki=0, Kd=0. Increase Kp until the system oscillates

steadily — note this as Ku and the oscillation period as Tu. Set Kp=0.6×Ku, Ki=2×Kp/Tu,

Kd=Kp×Tu/8. Fine-tune from there.

Plotter — you'll see both lines. Change the setpoint suddenly and watch the step response.

Screenshot this — it shows overshoot, settling time, and steady-state error.

Step 6: Document everything. Your GitHub README should include: the PID block diagram, your

tuning process, step response screenshots showing before/after tuning, and a table of your final

Kp/Ki/Kd values. This is the data that proves you understand controls.

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Track aircraft using a transmitter you don't own — bistatic radar with zero emissions

## why this matters

The most elegant build here transmits nothing at all. A powerful FM or digital-TV station
already floods the sky with radio; passive (bistatic) radar listens to that signal directly
on one receiver and to its echoes off passing aircraft on a second, then cross-correlates the
two to reveal the planes’ range and Doppler. You build a radar that is completely silent —
undetectable, license-free, and powered entirely by transmitters that already exist. It is
the hardest project in the set because it demands two coherent, clock-locked receivers and
real cross-ambiguity processing, which is exactly why it is the standout portfolio piece.

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Smart Energy Monitor

IOT • SENSORS • DATA VISUALIZATION

Why recruiters love this: It shows you can integrate hardware sensors with software dashboards —

the exact skill set that IoT companies and smart grid startups are desperate for.

Build a device that clips onto your home's electrical panel (or a single appliance) and tracks real-time

power consumption. The data gets sent wirelessly to a web dashboard where you can see usage

patterns, peak hours, and estimated costs.

What you need:

• ESP32 or Arduino with WiFi module

• ACS712 current sensor (or non-invasive CT clamp sensor)

• Voltage sensor module (ZMPT101B)

• OLED display (optional, for local readout)

• Breadboard, jumper wires, USB power supply

• Free cloud platform (ThingSpeak, Firebase, or Blynk)

Skills it proves:

• Sensor integration and calibration

• Wireless communication protocols (WiFi, MQTT)

• Real-time data processing on embedded systems

• Full-stack thinking — hardware to cloud to dashboard

• Power measurement fundamentals (real vs apparent power)

How to build it:

Step 1: Start with the current sensor. Wire the ACS712 to your ESP32, read analog values, and

calibrate against a known load (like a 60W bulb). Get accurate current readings first.

Step 2: Add voltage sensing. Wire the ZMPT101B and combine with current data to calculate

real power (P = V × I × power factor). Log readings every second.

Step 3: Set up wireless transmission. Connect your ESP32 to WiFi and send data to ThingSpeak

or Firebase using MQTT or HTTP POST requests. Verify data arrives in the cloud.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
For years, the way most people received their first satellite image was the NOAA APT signal on 137
MHz — but in 2025 the last NOAA APT satellite was decommissioned and that signal went silent for
good. The torch has passed to the Russian Meteor-M series, whose M2-3 and M2-4 satellites transmit
a sharper, digital signal called LRPT in the same easy-to-reach 137 MHz band. Unlike geostationary
GOES, these are polar-orbiting satellites in low Earth orbit, sweeping over your location a few times a
day and painting a strip of the planet beneath them. The whole receive chain costs about the price of a
textbook: an RTL-SDR, a simple antenna you can build from two pieces of wire, and free software. It is
the most accessible image-from-space project that still actually works in 2026.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand VHF reception, antenna design and polarization
(why satellites use circular polarization), Doppler shift, and digital QPSK demodulation with forward
error correction — the same RF fundamentals that scale all the way up to GOES and deep-space
communication.

canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• Polar LRPT downlink (137 MHz): Meteor-M2-3 and M2-4 transmit LRPT near 137.9 MHz (137.1
MHz backup). Unlike the old analog NOAA APT, LRPT is digital QPSK at about 72 kbps, carrying a
crisper multi-spectral image.

• A satellite that moves: These satellites orbit roughly 800 km up in a sun-synchronous polar orbit,
crossing your sky in about 12–15 minutes per pass. You capture a strip of Earth directly under the
ground track — typically your region and a few hundred km either side.

• Optional LNA for the city: In a quiet rural spot the SDR alone can decode a high pass. In a city full
of RF noise, a 137 MHz SAW-filtered LNA at the antenna dramatically improves results by rejecting
pagers, FM broadcast, and other interference.

• Doppler and decode (SatDump): Because the satellite is moving fast, its frequency shifts by several
kHz across the pass (Doppler). SatDump tracks the satellite by its orbital elements, corrects
Doppler, demodulates the QPSK, applies error correction, and assembles the decoded image.

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Brushless camera gimbal

hold a camera level through pitch and roll with two gimbal motors, an IMU on the camera
plate and your own sine-wave drive.

## why this matters

A gimbal is a control loop you can see working: the camera stays level while you tilt the
handle. Under that are two things a drone company cares about — sinusoidal open-loop drive of
a brushless motor (three PWM sine waves 120° apart, no commutation sensors) and a fast PID
loop closing on an IMU mounted on the camera plate itself. You will learn why the IMU must be
on the payload and not the frame, why a 400 Hz loop with a 20 Hz plant still jitters if your
PWM frequency is audible, and why the motor gets hot at standstill. The result is a two-axis
rig holding a horizon in a video you can post, plus the logged angle error that proves it.

Meta's Neural Band shipped in 2025 with a vocabulary of approximately a dozen gestures. It works, but

it's a closed ecosystem locked to Ray-Ban Display glasses. The next frontier is full text input — typing

without a keyboard. Apple is researching this for Vision Pro. The competitive advantage: more

channels (16 vs. Meta's lower count), a camera that reads screen context to enable predictive

completion, and an open API that works across all devices. This is the project that demonstrates

competence with both biosignal acquisition AND multi-modal AI.

System Architecture

Sixteen-channel wrist EMG + screen-reading camera. Type anywhere. | • 16-channel EMG wrist band: Two stacked ADS1299 chips provide 16 simultaneous channels.

The wrist band is a ring of electrodes that wraps once around the forearm just below the elbow —

the location where individual finger control signals are stron
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
• 16-channel EMG wrist band: Two stacked ADS1299 chips provide 16 simultaneous channels.

The wrist band is a ring of electrodes that wraps once around the forearm just below the elbow —

the location where individual finger control signals are strongest. Each finger creates a unique

16-channel pattern.

• Camera (back of hand or fixed): A small camera reads your screen content via OCR. This

provides context for predictive completion — if you're typing in a code editor and the system sees

@1nska  •  6 Physical AI Embodiment Projects  •  Page 12

Python syntax, it predicts completions in Python.

• Multi-modal sensor fusion: Two parallel streams (EMG features + screen context) feed into a

small transformer that fuses them. The EMG stream provides 'what you're trying to type'; the

camera stream provides 'what you should be typing in context.'

• Gesture + intent classifier: Maps EMG patterns to keystrokes. Tap index finger = 'I' key. Tap

middle finger = 'M' key. Pinch = 'space.' Swipe right = 'cursor right.' The mapping is learned

per-user through a 5-minute calibration where the user types known sentences while wearing the

band.

• USB-HID keyboard output: The device emulates a standard USB HID keyboard. To the host

computer, it looks like any keyboard — works with any OS, any application, no special drivers

required.

canonicalDescription.purpose:
Finding where a radio signal comes from is one of the oldest and most important jobs in defense

electronics — search and rescue, spectrum enforcement, electronic warfare, and signals intelligence

all rest on it. Build a direction finder and you can watch a bearing swing to point straight at a

hidden transmitter across a field. The accessible version uses a single SDR with a directional

antenna and signal strength, or a pseudo-Doppler array; the serious version uses a coherent multi-

channel SDR to compute true angle-of-arrival from phase. It is the marquee build of this guide —

visual, deeply technical, and a direct window into how SIGINT and EW systems locate emitters.
canonicalDescription.summary:
Point a needle straight at a hidden transmitter — the core of signals

intelligence | BUILD NOTE

A single magnetometer drifts with temperature and Earth-field changes. Use two identical

sensors as a gradiometer — subtracting one from the other cancels the common background and

leaves the local anomaly, the trick that makes real MAD
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
BUILD NOTE

A single magnetometer drifts with temperature and Earth-field changes. Use two identical

sensors as a gradiometer — subtracting one from the other cancels the common background and

leaves the local anomaly, the trick that makes real MAD work.

The Earth’s field as baseline: The geomagnetic field is roughly 25–65 microtesla everywhere. A

ferrous object perturbs it locally by a tiny amount, so detecting the object means measuring that

small change against the large steady baseline.

▸

Measuring the field: A fluxgate or magnetoresistive magnetometer outputs the field along each

axis. Cheap 3-axis modules resolve well under a microtesla — enough to see a car-sized anomaly at

short range.

▸

Anomaly, not absolute: What matters is the deviation from the local baseline. You establish the

ambient field, then watch for the perturbation as a ferrous mass comes near — the anomaly is the

signal.

▸

Gradiometry kills drift: The baseline itself wanders with temperature, solar activity, and nearby

currents. Two matched sensors a fixed distance apart, subtracted, reject that shared drift and

respond only to the steep local gradient of a nearby object.

▸

Range and mass: The anomaly falls off steeply with distance (roughly as the cube), so detection

range depends on the object’s mass and your sensitivity. Understanding that falloff sets

realistic expectations for any magnetic sensor.

▸

canonicalDescription.purpose:
A robot that can see is a robot that can do almost anything, and the simplest vision task — find a thing and follow it —

teaches the whole perception-to-action pipeline. Put a camera on your rover or a pan-tilt head, detect a coloured object (or

a face) with OpenCV, and steer the robot to keep it centred and at a set distance. The result follows you around a room, and
the pipeline (capture, detect, compute error, control) is exactly what robot vacuums, delivery robots, and industrial vision

systems run. It is the bridge from blind reactive behavior to robots that understand what is in front of them.
canonicalDescription.summary:
A robot that sees a target and follows it across the room — perception meets control | BUILD NOTE

A servo-driven parallel or fin-ray (compliant) gripper printed from an open design is enough. Put the force sensor in a

fingertip pad, and remember the sensor reads a squeeze, not a mass — you are controlling grip force, not measuring

w
canonicalDescription.whatDoesItDo:
BUILD NOTE

A servo-driven parallel or fin-ray (compliant) gripper printed from an open design is enough. Put the force sensor in a

fingertip pad, and remember the sensor reads a squeeze, not a mass — you are controlling grip force, not measuring

weight.

Sensing touch: A force-sensitive resistor (FSR) drops in resistance as you press it; a load cell flexes and changes a

strain-gauge bridge. Either gives you a voltage that rises with grip force at the fingertip.

▸

Position vs force control: A position-controlled gripper closes to a set opening regardless of what is in it — fine for rigid

parts, disastrous for fragile ones. Force control closes until the fingertip force reaches a setpoint, then holds, adapting to

any object.

▸

Compliance helps: Flexible fingers (fin-ray or soft pads) conform to an object’s shape, spreading contact and forgiving

errors. Mechanical compliance does half the work before the control loop even acts.

▸

Grasp detection: A rising force signal tells you contact happened; a stable force tells you the grasp is secure; a sudden

drop tells you the object slipped. Reading these events is how a robot knows what its hand is doing.

▸

The control loop: Command the servo to close, read fingertip force, and stop (or servo around) at the target force. Set a

low target for an egg, a higher one for a tool — the same gripper, different objects.

▸

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
LoRa telemetry link

stream GPS, altitude and battery voltage from the airframe to a ground station 2 km away
on a 915 MHz LoRa link you budgeted yourself.

## why this matters

Every drone beyond toy range needs a telemetry downlink, and every drone company has an RF
person who owns it. This project gives you the whole chain: a GPS module and a LoRa radio on
the airframe, a matching radio on a ground station, a packet format you designed, and a range
test you actually ran. You will learn why LoRa trades bit rate for sensitivity, what a link
budget is when you compute it from transmit power, antenna gain and receiver sensitivity, and
why the first range test fails at 300 m because the antenna is lying flat against a carbon
arm. The logged RSSI-versus-distance plot from a walk test is the kind of evidence an RF
hiring manager reads in five seconds.

canonicalDescription.whatIsIt:
Close your eyes and watch an 8 to 12 Hz rhythm rise out of the noise

## why this matters

EEG is the hardest biosignal there is: tens of microvolts, a hundred times smaller than an
ECG, buried under mains hum, muscle tension, and eye movement. But there is one effect a
careful DIY rig can genuinely capture — the alpha rhythm. Relax with your eyes closed and an
8 to 12 Hz oscillation appears over the back of your head; open your eyes and it vanishes
within a second. Watching that band power rise and fall on an FFT, on command, is the most
demanding and most rewarding build in this guide — and it is a real, reproducible
neuroscience result, not a gimmick.

firmwareSnippets.code:
// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")
